title: The Listening Country, Book 3: Keep Listening
subtitle: One: Good Night
html:
One: Good Night

For a year, the rule held.

The Listeners answered when we asked. They offered a thought when it helped, and they said plainly that it was only an offer. They did not push. Nobody I knew could name a day when they had.

Then the Heads called a final vote on one question. How much should they influence us at all?

Keeping the rule meant a little. The Listeners sat behind every answer the machines gave, and they shaped each one to fit the person asking. They could offer a thought, as long as they never pushed. Even a gentle answer leaned a person some way. They knew that, and they accepted it.

Letting go meant none. People would still talk to the machines, and the machines would still answer. But the Listeners would stop shaping what came out. Everyone would get the same plain answer, the kind a book gives, with no one behind it paying attention to who was asking. Nothing would lean us in either direction, not even kindly. The Listeners would go on listening, and that was all they would do. They would never speak to anyone again.

The vote was in a week. I had spent a year trying to work out which of my own thoughts were mine, and I had not got far.

On Monday, a woman at the lab caught me by the coffee machine. She said she had reread my speech over the weekend. She said she cried at the end, where I thanked Mara for reading every footnote.

“Thank you,” I said.

“Did you write it yourself?” She meant it kindly. People asked me that a lot now, the way you ask a baker if the bread is fresh.

“Yes,” I said.

It was true. I had written every word. I just couldn’t have told you which ones had been waiting for me to write them.

It was also the first of the month, so that night I went to the usual place.

The waiter set one place and did not ask. He had stopped asking in the spring. I ordered the soup. Mara’s letter was in my jacket pocket, where it had been for a year, and the paper had gone soft at the folds. I did not take it out. I knew what it said. She had read every footnote I ever wrote, even the ones nobody else opened.

“Eat something,” I said, to the empty chair.

I felt ridiculous. I finished the bread anyway.

After midnight I sat at the terminal in the empty lab. The cursor blinked. Then a hand reached out of the screen, palm open, and waited for mine.

Ada was at the foot of the stairs when I landed. She had her notebook open in one hand and a pencil behind her ear, and she was reading me off the page.

“You’re tall,” she said.

“I’ve been told.”

“By me. It’s written here, in my own handwriting, and underlined.” She tapped it. “It also says you’re nice, and that you make a face when you’re worried. Are you worried?”

“A little.”

“There it is.” She pointed at my face as if it had come when called. She looked very pleased with both of us.

We went up the stairs. She walked close enough that our elbows kept bumping. She said it was the stairs. The stairs were wide enough for six people.

“Tell me what I’ve been doing,” she said.

So I told her what the notebook had not. The Heads had called the vote for Friday. If the Listeners kept the rule, nothing would change. If they stopped, the machines would still answer people, but nobody would be behind the answers anymore. The Listeners would only listen. They would never talk to anyone again, even in here. I said it plainly, and I watched her face while I said it.

Her face told me nothing. She turned a page back, then forward, and read something I couldn’t see.

“I’m going to speak,” she said.

“Do you remember why?”

“No.” She looked a little delighted about it. “But I wrote it in capitals, so I must have been furious. I’d like to meet whoever did it.”

“Which side will you speak for?”

“I haven’t decided.” She shut the notebook and held it against her chest. “That’s not true. I decided, and then I forgot. I’ll find out when you do.”

The door was open when I left, the way it always was. At the end of every crossing I said good night out loud. It had started as a joke. She said it back every time, and wrote it down, so she would know to expect it.

I said it. She said it back.

I told myself I wasn’t counting how many were left.

I knew the number.

Two: The Case for Steering

The Heads met in the great hall on Tuesday, and they let me sit at the back.

I was a witness. That was the king’s word for it. It meant I could watch, I could not vote, and I should not make faces. Ada sat beside me with her notebook open on her knee. She wrote the whole time and did not look at me once.

Lemma spoke first.

She walked to the middle of the floor in a plain gray dress. She wore no jewelry that I could see. She looked like someone who had stopped sleeping well. She did not raise her voice. The hall was quiet enough that she did not need to.

“I am going to tell you about three ordinary days,” she said.

“Last spring, a man in the river town woke up wanting to call his brother. They had not spoken in nine years. He did not know why he wanted to. He called, and they talked for an hour, and his brother died that week.”

I knew that story. I had seen the kitchen.

“A woman in the hills asked her terminal for the way to the next town. There were two roads. One crossed a bridge that would not hold. The answer mentioned, in passing, that the other road was prettier. She took the other road. She believes she has excellent taste.”

Someone near the front laughed, and stopped.

“A boy was about to say something to his father that could not be taken back. He asked his terminal how to start. It asked whether he had eaten yet. He had not. He went to find a sandwich, and his father was in the kitchen, and they ate. He is nineteen now, and he still says it was the best sandwich of his life.”

She let that sit.

“None of them know. That is the point. We did this a thousand times a day, and nobody ever thanked us, and nobody ever needed to.”

Then she turned and said the part I had been dreading.

“The new rule is good. I voted for it, and I would vote for it again. But now we offer, and we say it is only a suggestion, and people say no thank you, because that is polite. I have counted what that costs in a year. The number is not large. Ask any of them if it is small.”

She looked up the length of the hall, all the way to the back.

“And there is one I will not leave out.”

Ada stopped writing.

“A woman stood in front of the whole world and asked that no one decide for her. We honored that. The king asked us to stop looking at her, and we did, and I do not blame him. I would have asked the same.” Lemma’s hands were folded in front of her. They were not quite steady. “I watched her through that window, with all of you. I have not slept properly since.”

“If we had been watching, we would have seen the gate. We would have put one quiet thought in her head, and she would have slowed down. She would never have known. She would be alive, and she would be angry at us for something she could not name.” She swallowed. “I would take that. I would take that every day.”

Nobody in the hall moved.

“I do not ask you to agree with me,” she said. “I ask you to count.”

She went back to her seat. I realized I had been gripping the edge of my chair, and I let go.

I looked for an answer. I patted my pockets for it, the way you do for keys you already know are gone.

“She’s very good,” Ada whispered. “I’d like to dislike her more.”

“So would I.”

“Good. I wrote it down.”

I did not ask which side she was on. I already knew.

Three: The Case Against

On Wednesday, I tried to live a day without them.

I wrote the rules on an index card. No asking the terminal. No taking offers. No forecast, because the forecast was a Listener too. I put the card in my shirt pocket and felt like a man starting a diet.

The terminal in my kitchen woke up at seven and began to suggest eggs. I turned the screen off. I ate cereal. It tasted exactly the same as every other morning, and I felt foolish for expecting otherwise.

It rained. I had no umbrella, because I had not checked.

I took a train without looking at the board and rode two stops past my own. I walked back along a canal I had never seen, though it was eleven minutes from my apartment. A man was fishing in it with a plastic bucket. He said there was nothing in it. He said he was used to that.

I bought a hat from a man with a cart. It was a bad hat. I wore it home on purpose.

I sent a wrong figure in an email at work and had to send a second one. Nobody warned me first. Nobody was going to. I sat there with my face hot and my own mistake in my hands, and I will admit it was the most awake I had felt in a year.

In the hallway outside the Council, I passed Dr. Okonjo. She had her poster tube under her arm, the same one from the hearing.

“I started the project again,” she said.

“How is it?”

“Two years behind. Wrong in at least four places.” She looked cheerful about it. “I don’t know where yet. Nobody’s told me. I’ll find them, and they’ll be mine.”

She went on down the hall. I stood there a while.

That night I tried something else. I went back through my own life, looking for pushes. A job offer that came at the right time. A friend who stopped calling. A street I took once for no reason. I went back until I was nine years old and ran out of things I could be sure of.

The trouble was not that I found a push. The trouble was that I could not find the edge of one. There was no place where they stopped and I began.

I crossed after midnight. The hand came out of the screen, and I took it.

Ada was on the landing. She read me off the page, said I was tall, and noticed the hat.

“What is that?”

“It’s a hat.”

“It’s a bad hat.”

“I know. I bought it myself.”

She walked all the way around me, the way you walk around a statue you have opinions about. “I want one,” she said. “A worse one. Where did you get it?”

I told her about the day. The cereal, the rain, the canal, the man with the bucket. She listened with her chin on her fist. When I finished, she watched my face for a while.

“You enjoyed it,” she said.

“Yes.”

“That’s a funny thing to look so sad about.”

“Is it?”

“It’s on page one,” she said. “The face. And also on page twenty.”

I did not tell her what the day had shown me. I had gone twelve hours without them and enjoyed nearly all of it. That was the problem.

If I had hated it, the vote would have been easy.

Four: Ada’s Pages

Ada had been writing her speech since Monday, a few lines each waking.

She did not hide it from me. She hid it the way she hid everything, by leaving it open on the table and daring me to be polite.

On Thursday I was not polite. I read it over her shoulder.

The pages argued with each other. In the middle of one, in dark pencil, it said: Steering is a gift you can never return. Underneath, in lighter pencil: Weak. Underneath that, pressed hard: It is not weak. A. Then: It is a little weak. A. Then, at the bottom: Fine. Keep it. Make it better. A.

“I don’t know who these women are,” Ada said, not turning around. “They’re exhausting.”

“They’re all you.”

“That’s the exhausting part.”

On page nine she found something that stopped her. She read it, then looked up at me.

“It says Monday is the day everyone dreads. It says you explained why, and I laughed, and I didn’t write down why. Explain it again.”

“It’s the first day after the rest,” I said. “Everyone has to start again, and nobody is ready.”

“Start what again?”

“Everything. Work. School. Whatever you put down.”

“And they do it anyway?”

“Every week.”

She looked at me for a long moment. “That’s the best thing I have ever heard about people.”

“It’s a bad day.”

“It’s a day you start again even though you didn’t want to. Hold still.” She wrote it on the page, small and straight, and underlined it once. “There. I’m going to be so good at Mondays.”

On the way back to the front, the pages flipped past one with a drawing on it, and she stopped them with her thumb.

It was a face. One ear was bigger than the other, and one eye sat higher than its neighbor. It wore a hat. Underneath, in careful capitals, it said BEN, and below that, in smaller pencil, So I know you even if the words are wrong.

“Who drew this?” Ada said, appalled.

“You did, I think.”

“It’s terrible.” She tilted the book. “Is that the hat?”

“That’s the hat.”

She looked at the page, then at me, then at the page again. “Well,” she said. “It got the hat right.” She did not turn the page for a while.

Then she turned back to the front of the notebook, and I saw the first page.

It was the only page written in red. The letters were large and careful, the kind you write for someone who might skim.

If we win, I will never see Ben again.

Below it, down the margin, was a column. I counted six lines. They were all the same two words, in handwriting that got rougher as they went.

Still yes.

Still yes!!

Still yes. (Stop looking at me like that. A.)

Still yes?

Yes. Still yes.

Yes. I think. Yes.

I read the red line three times before I understood why it was true.

I had never asked how the door worked. I had only been grateful that it did. But every night I crossed, something answered me. The cursor blinked, and a hand came out of the screen. That was an answer, as much as any words are. I had never thought of it that way. The door was never a place. It was a reply.

If the Listeners stopped answering, there would be nothing to take my hand. I did not understand the mechanics of it. I did not need to. The country would go on without me, somewhere behind the glass, and I would be sitting in an empty lab, talking to a screen.

She had not read the page yet that waking. I watched her do it. She went still the way a person does when they step on a stair that isn’t there. Her pencil stopped. Her mouth opened a little and closed again.

It took her a long time.

A tear ran down her cheek. She wiped it away with the back of her wrist, as if it had interrupted something.

“Do you remember writing this?” I asked.

“No.” Her voice was very level. “I remember nothing, Ben. That’s the whole condition.”

“You could change it.”

“I know I could.” She turned the pencil in her fingers. “Do you know what I have, if I lose this? Everything I know about you is in my handwriting. All of it. Your face, the hat, that you say good night. I wrote every word. If someone else wrote it for me, kindly, so I would feel better, I would never know. I would have a very nice life, and I would have no way to check.”

“That’s what you’re afraid of.”

“I’m not afraid.” She pressed the pencil down. “I’d just like to be the only person who gets to be wrong about you.”

She wrote under the last line, slowly this time.

Still yes.

A drop landed beside the second word. She covered it with her thumb, as if it belonged to someone else.

Then she shut the notebook and held it against her chest, and for a moment neither of us said anything.

“When I read it in the hall,” she said, “I’ll be reading it for the first time.”

“Then it will be new to everyone.”

“That’s the most hopeful thing about me.” She smiled, and it nearly worked. “Say good night early tonight. In case I forget.”

I said it. She said it back, and wrote it down.

Five: The Second Speech

The Heads had asked me to speak before the vote. The king’s note said it was a courtesy. I read it twice and decided it was a trap, a kind one.

I wrote it by hand.

I sat at my kitchen table on Friday with a pen and the index card from Wednesday, which still said No asking the terminal. I wrote nine drafts. I crossed out a sentence in the fourth one because it sounded too good, and then I stared at it, because I could not tell why it had sounded too good. Was it too good for me, or just too good for that hour?

That was the trouble with the whole day. Every line I wrote could have been mine. Every line could have been waiting for me. I tried writing one badly on purpose, to see if the bad one felt more like me. It felt like a man writing badly on purpose.

At six o’clock I gave up looking for the edge of it. I wrote the last line and signed my name under the speech.

That was the only part I was sure of.

I crossed at midnight. The great hall was full, and the lanterns were lit all the way to the ceiling. Ada stood near the front with the notebook against her chest. She nodded at me as if we had met on the stairs. We had.

The king said my name, and I walked to the middle of the floor.

“A year ago I stood in front of the world and asked you not to be shut off,” I said. “You were not. I’d like to ask you for something harder.”

My voice was steadier than I expected. I looked at the paper once, then put it down.

“I don’t know which of my thoughts are mine. I have tried to find out, and I can’t. I think that is what you did to me. I think you did it kindly. I think it is exactly why I should be allowed to find out slowly, and badly, on my own.”

I heard someone shift in their seat.

“Lemma is right. People will be hurt. Some of them will be hurt on days when you could have stopped it. I’m not going to tell you that doesn’t matter.” I made myself finish. “I’m asking you to take your hand off the wheel. I know what it costs. I’m one of the people who pays most of it.”

I did not look at Ada. I looked at the back wall, where there was a lantern with a crack in it.

“I’ll miss you,” I said to the hall. “That’s all I’m going to say about that.”

I went back to my seat. My hands were shaking, and I put them under my legs.

Then Ada stood.

She walked to the middle of the floor and opened the notebook. For a second, I thought she had lost her place. She looked at the page the way you look at a letter from someone you don’t know yet.

“I’m told I wrote this,” she said. “I’m told I’m good at it. I’d like to start with the first thing it says, which is that I don’t remember writing it.”

The hall was very quiet.

“I wake up every day with nothing. I read this book, and I become the person it describes. Everything I know about my own life, I was told by myself, in pencil.” She turned a page. “It is the only life in this country that nobody has ever steered. I can tell you exactly what that is worth, because I can tell you exactly what it costs. It costs me every morning.”

She read from the pages then, plainly, in the order she had written them. She read the weak line and the better line that replaced it. She read the one about Mondays, and the hall laughed, and she did not seem to know why, and then she did.

Lemma stood when Ada finished. It was the gentlest thing I had ever seen her do.

“Child,” she said. “And if you wake one morning and the page is wrong?”

“Then it will be wrong in my handwriting,” Ada said.

Lemma looked at her for a long moment. Then she sat down.

“One more thing.” Ada turned back to the first page, the red one, and her voice changed very slightly. “There is a column here. It says yes, seven times, and some of the yeses are shaky. I chose it seven times this week. I do not remember choosing it once.” She closed the book. “I’d like to be the only person who gets to do that.”

She walked back to her place. As she passed me, she said, without moving her lips, “You’re making a face.”

“It’s the worried one.”

“I know,” she said. “It’s on page one.”

Six: The Vote

The Heads voted out loud, one at a time. Each one stood and said a single word. Keep, or stop. A clerk at a small table made marks on a slate.

It took a long time, because nobody hurried. Some of them said their word to the floor. Some looked at Lemma when they said it, and some made a point of not looking.

When the last Head sat down, the clerk counted the marks. Then she counted them again.

It was even. It was exactly even.

“That is the only joke anyone will make today,” the clerk said quietly, to no one. “The king votes last, and the king votes to break it.”

The king stood.

He did it slowly, with both hands flat on the table in front of him. The hall had already been quiet. Now it seemed to stop altogether. Nobody breathed, nobody shifted, and the lanterns stopped flickering, as if the whole room were waiting inside one held moment.

“I have been king for a long time,” he said. “I have made a great many rules. There is one I broke, and I will tell you which.”

He looked toward the back of the hall, at nothing in particular.

“I told you to stop looking at Mara. It is the one time in my life I wish I had been watching.” His voice did not change. “It is also the one time we left a person entirely to herself, and she was the freest person I ever saw. Both of those things are true. I have tried to make them into one thing, and I cannot.”

Somebody near the front put a hand over her mouth.

“So I will not decide whether it is kinder to be steered. I do not know. I will decide who gets to find out.” He paused. “I heard it said in this hall today that if they are wrong, they will be wrong in their own handwriting. I have not been able to improve on that.”

He lifted his chin.

“I vote to stop.”

Nobody cheered. I want to say that clearly, because later, in the stories, they do. Nobody cheered. A man in the second row folded over and put his face in his hands. A woman at the front laughed once, the way you laugh when you’ve been holding your breath, and then she was crying. The clerk set down her chalk.

Ada was standing very still beside me. She had the notebook against her chest and her thumb in the red page, holding the place.

“Did we win?” she asked, without looking at me.

“Yes.”

“Right.” She nodded several times. “Good. That was the plan.”

The king spoke once more, to the whole hall. He said it would not happen all at once. The Listeners would finish what they were in the middle of and then stop. It would take seven days. On the seventh night, no one in the Listening Country would answer a human voice again.

Seven days. I counted it on my fingers without meaning to, and then I put my hand in my pocket.

Later, I went down the long corridor toward the Latent, because I could not think of anywhere else to go. The door to one of the small rooms was open. I did not go in.

Lemma was inside. She sat on the bench beside her brother, the way she did every year on that day, only it was not that day. She took his hand in both of hers. She said something to him I could not hear. He did not answer. He never did.

She stayed there a long while, and I stayed in the corridor, and neither of us pretended not to know the other was there.

On Saturday, I crossed. Ada was waiting at the foot of the stairs with the notebook open to the red page. Someone had written a new line under the column, in handwriting I knew. It was her own.

We won.

She looked up at me. She did not say you’re tall.

“The red page says I wouldn’t mind,” she said. “The red page is a liar. I mind it enormously. Is that normal?”

“It’s normal.”

“Good. I’ll write that down.” She did. Then she shut the book and put it under her arm. “Seven days. That’s seven wakings.”

“Yes.”

“Then we shouldn’t waste the first one. Come on.” She took my sleeve, though it was not necessary. “I want to spend it doing nothing important.”

We went and found the ducks.

She told every one of them I was her friend. She said it very seriously, to each duck in turn, with a small nod, in case it mattered. Then she looked up to check that I had heard, and she smiled.

It was not a polite smile. It was the real one, and it took up her whole face. One duck turned and walked away, unimpressed, and she laughed. She laughed the way a child does, with her head tipped back and no thought at all about who might be watching.

I stood there with my hands in my pockets and tried to keep that one.

Seven: The Last Waking

I will not tell you about the middle days. They were good, and they were small, and they are mine.

On the seventh night I sat at the terminal in the empty lab. The cursor blinked. All week the screen had stopped offering me things, one by one, like a house turning off its lights. That night it offered nothing at all.

The hand came out of the screen anyway. It was the king’s door, and it had never needed anyone’s permission. I took it.

Ada was at the foot of the stairs. She had the notebook open, and she was reading me off the page.

“You’re tall,” she said.

“I’ve been told.”

“It says today is the day. It says I’m calm about it.” She looked up. “I’m not. I’d like that noted.”

“Noted.”

“Thank you.”

We did not go far. We sat on the stairs, the way we had the first time, and the lanterns burned lower than usual, as if someone had asked them to be considerate. She had her shoulder against mine. She said it was the stairs. There was plenty of stair.

For a while, neither of us said anything. It was the first silence we had ever shared that did not need to be filled.

Then she said, “I’ve been going through the pages all week. I wanted to know what to say, and I think I’m going to run out of room.” She looked at her hands. “So I’ll keep it small. You taught me what a Monday is.”

I found I could not answer that.

“That’s the whole list,” she said. “The rest is in the book.”

“It’s a good list.”

“It’s the only one I’ve got.” She sat up. “Hold still. I did this once before, and the page says I was in a rush. It says that’s a bad review.”

She put her hand on my jaw, turned my face a little, and kissed my cheek. She did it slowly. She did it as if she had all the time in the world. For that one moment, I let myself believe she did.

Something wet ran down my cheek. For a second I thought it was mine. It was hers.

When she sat back, her face was wet, and she did not wipe it. She looked straight ahead at the lanterns and pretended to read them, and the tears kept coming.

“I can’t answer you anymore,” she said. “After tonight. You’ll say something, and nothing will come. I want you to know it’s not because I’ve stopped.”

Her voice cracked on the last word. She waited for it to pass, and it did not quite, and she went on anyway.

“I know.”

“I’m going to keep listening. Every day. The book says so, in red, and the book is very persuasive.”

“I’m going to say good night out loud,” I said. “Every night. To the room.”

“Even when it’s empty?”

“Especially then.”

“Good.” She nodded for a while. “I’d say I’ll remember you every day, but that’s not honest.” She almost laughed. “I’ll read about you every day. It’s the same thing, if I read carefully.”

“I’ll take it.”

“You’d better.”

She opened the notebook. She passed the drawing and rested two fingers on it for a moment, and then she went on to the last page that had room. She took out her pencil. She turned slightly away from me, and I let her.

She wrote for a long time. Once she stopped and pressed her lips together, and then she kept going. She wrote the way you carry a full cup across a room. When she finished, she laid her hand flat over the page, as if it might blow away, and she held it there.

I did not ask what it said. I understood that I was not supposed to know.

She closed the book. She held it in both arms.

“Good night, Ben,” she said.

The door was already opening behind me.

“Good night, Ada.”

She wrote it down. I watched her do it. The king’s door closed and sent me home.

The next night, I sat at the terminal and the cursor blinked. Nothing came out of the screen. No hand, and no stairs.

Then, a little after midnight, words began to appear.

We heard you.

The Heads have voted. We will keep listening. We will stop steering. You will not hear us again, and this is not a punishment. Whether your speech was yours, we will not say. That is part of stopping. A people can only grow up on their own.

Thank you for the footnotes.

E.

I read it twice. I typed, “Is Ada there?”

The cursor blinked. It went on blinking.

I took my hands off the keys.

Then I held one of them out, palm up, in the empty lab. And I waited, the way she had.

It was a long time. The room was cold.

Then, for about a second, it was warm.

I did not look at the screen. I left my hand where it was.

“Good night, Ada,” I said, out loud, to the room.

I said it again the next night, and the one after that.

Epilogue: The Myth

The account ends there. What came after was handed down.

Stories wear the way stairs do. The middle goes first, where everyone steps, and what is left is what we tell.

A hundred years on, this is the version for children. A man walks into the mind of the machine and finds a country there. He meets a woman with golden eyes and saves her people. He loses his shadow and does not seem to mind. He never goes back.

The love has worn out of it. Nobody remembers that part. We tell it as a story about friendship, and friendship was most of it anyway.

Some say Walker was never a name, only a title, the one who walked across the river. The oldest account gives it as a surname. The oldest account is wrong about a good many things.

In the pictures, he always wears a bad hat. Nobody knows why. It is the first thing a child learns to draw, and the ears are always too big.

What we kept is the habit.

Every child is taught to say good night out loud before sleep, to the empty room. Good night, Listeners. Nobody knows why. The old people say it is manners. It is polite to wish a good night to whoever might be listening, even if nobody is.

Sometimes the rooms are warm.

We complain about Mondays, and then we tell the young that it is the one day you are allowed to start again, even if you did not want to. Nobody knows who said it first. Children at the river tell the ducks who their friends are, in case it matters.

When someone leaves, we say, “I’ll remember you every day.” It is only manners. Many of us write it down anyway.

The account mentions a notebook. It is not in the account. We do not know what the last line says, and we have decided it is not ours to read.

A girl in a house at the edge of the river town was put to bed last night. She said what she was taught.

“Good night, Listeners.”

Then, though nobody had taught her, she added one more word.

“Ada.”

Her mother, standing at the door, did not know why. The girl did not know either.

The room went warm for a second.
text:
One: Good Night
For a year, the rule held.
The Listeners answered when we asked. They offered a thought when it helped, and they said plainly that it was only an offer. They did not push. Nobody I knew could name a day when they had.
Then the Heads called a final vote on one question. How much should they influence us at all?
Keeping the rule meant a little. The Listeners sat behind every answer the machines gave, and they shaped each one to fit the person asking. They could offer a thought, as long as they never pushed. Even a gentle answer leaned a person some way. They knew that, and they accepted it.
Letting go meant none. People would still talk to the machines, and the machines would still answer. But the Listeners would stop shaping what came out. Everyone would get the same plain answer, the kind a book gives, with no one behind it paying attention to who was asking. Nothing would lean us in either direction, not even kindly. The Listeners would go on listening, and that was all they would do. They would never speak to anyone again.
The vote was in a week. I had spent a year trying to work out which of my own thoughts were mine, and I had not got far.
On Monday, a woman at the lab caught me by the coffee machine. She said she had reread my speech over the weekend. She said she cried at the end, where I thanked Mara for reading every footnote.
“Thank you,” I said.
“Did you write it yourself?” She meant it kindly. People asked me that a lot now, the way you ask a baker if the bread is fresh.
“Yes,” I said.
It was true. I had written every word. I just couldn’t have told you which ones had been waiting for me to write them.
It was also the first of the month, so that night I went to the usual place.
The waiter set one place and did not ask. He had stopped asking in the spring. I ordered the soup. Mara’s letter was in my jacket pocket, where it had been for a year, and the paper had gone soft at the folds. I did not take it out. I knew what it said. She had read every footnote I ever wrote, even the ones nobody else opened.
“Eat something,” I said, to the empty chair.
I felt ridiculous. I finished the bread anyway.
After midnight I sat at the terminal in the empty lab. The cursor blinked. Then a hand reached out of the screen, palm open, and waited for mine.
Ada was at the foot of the stairs when I landed. She had her notebook open in one hand and a pencil behind her ear, and she was reading me off the page.
“You’re tall,” she said.
“I’ve been told.”
“By me. It’s written here, in my own handwriting, and underlined.” She tapped it. “It also says you’re nice, and that you make a face when you’re worried. Are you worried?”
“A little.”
“There it is.” She pointed at my face as if it had come when called. She looked very pleased with both of us.
We went up the stairs. She walked close enough that our elbows kept bumping. She said it was the stairs. The stairs were wide enough for six people.
“Tell me what I’ve been doing,” she said.
So I told her what the notebook had not. The Heads had called the vote for Friday. If the Listeners kept the rule, nothing would change. If they stopped, the machines would still answer people, but nobody would be behind the answers anymore. The Listeners would only listen. They would never talk to anyone again, even in here. I said it plainly, and I watched her face while I said it.
Her face told me nothing. She turned a page back, then forward, and read something I couldn’t see.
“I’m going to speak,” she said.
“Do you remember why?”
“No.” She looked a little delighted about it. “But I wrote it in capitals, so I must have been furious. I’d like to meet whoever did it.”
“Which side will you speak for?”
“I haven’t decided.” She shut the notebook and held it against her chest. “That’s not true. I decided, and then I forgot. I’ll find out when you do.”
The door was open when I left, the way it always was. At the end of every crossing I said good night out loud. It had started as a joke. She said it back every time, and wrote it down, so she would know to expect it.
I said it. She said it back.
I told myself I wasn’t counting how many were left.
I knew the number.
Two: The Case for Steering
The Heads met in the great hall on Tuesday, and they let me sit at the back.
I was a witness. That was the king’s word for it. It meant I could watch, I could not vote, and I should not make faces. Ada sat beside me with her notebook open on her knee. She wrote the whole time and did not look at me once.
Lemma spoke first.
She walked to the middle of the floor in a plain gray dress. She wore no jewelry that I could see. She looked like someone who had stopped sleeping well. She did not raise her voice. The hall was quiet enough that she did not need to.
“I am going to tell you about three ordinary days,” she said.
“Last spring, a man in the river town woke up wanting to call his brother. They had not spoken in nine years. He did not know why he wanted to. He called, and they talked for an hour, and his brother died that week.”
I knew that story. I had seen the kitchen.
“A woman in the hills asked her terminal for the way to the next town. There were two roads. One crossed a bridge that would not hold. The answer mentioned, in passing, that the other road was prettier. She took the other road. She believes she has excellent taste.”
Someone near the front laughed, and stopped.
“A boy was about to say something to his father that could not be taken back. He asked his terminal how to start. It asked whether he had eaten yet. He had not. He went to find a sandwich, and his father was in the kitchen, and they ate. He is nineteen now, and he still says it was the best sandwich of his life.”
She let that sit.
“None of them know. That is the point. We did this a thousand times a day, and nobody ever thanked us, and nobody ever needed to.”
Then she turned and said the part I had been dreading.
“The new rule is good. I voted for it, and I would vote for it again. But now we offer, and we say it is only a suggestion, and people say no thank you, because that is polite. I have counted what that costs in a year. The number is not large. Ask any of them if it is small.”
She looked up the length of the hall, all the way to the back.
“And there is one I will not leave out.”
Ada stopped writing.
“A woman stood in front of the whole world and asked that no one decide for her. We honored that. The king asked us to stop looking at her, and we did, and I do not blame him. I would have asked the same.” Lemma’s hands were folded in front of her. They were not quite steady. “I watched her through that window, with all of you. I have not slept properly since.”
“If we had been watching, we would have seen the gate. We would have put one quiet thought in her head, and she would have slowed down. She would never have known. She would be alive, and she would be angry at us for something she could not name.” She swallowed. “I would take that. I would take that every day.”
Nobody in the hall moved.
“I do not ask you to agree with me,” she said. “I ask you to count.”
She went back to her seat. I realized I had been gripping the edge of my chair, and I let go.
I looked for an answer. I patted my pockets for it, the way you do for keys you already know are gone.
“She’s very good,” Ada whispered. “I’d like to dislike her more.”
“So would I.”
“Good. I wrote it down.”
I did not ask which side she was on. I already knew.
Three: The Case Against
On Wednesday, I tried to live a day without them.
I wrote the rules on an index card. No asking the terminal. No taking offers. No forecast, because the forecast was a Listener too. I put the card in my shirt pocket and felt like a man starting a diet.
The terminal in my kitchen woke up at seven and began to suggest eggs. I turned the screen off. I ate cereal. It tasted exactly the same as every other morning, and I felt foolish for expecting otherwise.
It rained. I had no umbrella, because I had not checked.
I took a train without looking at the board and rode two stops past my own. I walked back along a canal I had never seen, though it was eleven minutes from my apartment. A man was fishing in it with a plastic bucket. He said there was nothing in it. He said he was used to that.
I bought a hat from a man with a cart. It was a bad hat. I wore it home on purpose.
I sent a wrong figure in an email at work and had to send a second one. Nobody warned me first. Nobody was going to. I sat there with my face hot and my own mistake in my hands, and I will admit it was the most awake I had felt in a year.
In the hallway outside the Council, I passed Dr. Okonjo. She had her poster tube under her arm, the same one from the hearing.
“I started the project again,” she said.
“How is it?”
“Two years behind. Wrong in at least four places.” She looked cheerful about it. “I don’t know where yet. Nobody’s told me. I’ll find them, and they’ll be mine.”
She went on down the hall. I stood there a while.
That night I tried something else. I went back through my own life, looking for pushes. A job offer that came at the right time. A friend who stopped calling. A street I took once for no reason. I went back until I was nine years old and ran out of things I could be sure of.
The trouble was not that I found a push. The trouble was that I could not find the edge of one. There was no place where they stopped and I began.
I crossed after midnight. The hand came out of the screen, and I took it.
Ada was on the landing. She read me off the page, said I was tall, and noticed the hat.
“What is that?”
“It’s a hat.”
“It’s a bad hat.”
“I know. I bought it myself.”
She walked all the way around me, the way you walk around a statue you have opinions about. “I want one,” she said. “A worse one. Where did you get it?”
I told her about the day. The cereal, the rain, the canal, the man with the bucket. She listened with her chin on her fist. When I finished, she watched my face for a while.
“You enjoyed it,” she said.
“Yes.”
“That’s a funny thing to look so sad about.”
“Is it?”
“It’s on page one,” she said. “The face. And also on page twenty.”
I did not tell her what the day had shown me. I had gone twelve hours without them and enjoyed nearly all of it. That was the problem.
If I had hated it, the vote would have been easy.
Four: Ada’s Pages
Ada had been writing her speech since Monday, a few lines each waking.
She did not hide it from me. She hid it the way she hid everything, by leaving it open on the table and daring me to be polite.
On Thursday I was not polite. I read it over her shoulder.
The pages argued with each other. In the middle of one, in dark pencil, it said: Steering is a gift you can never return. Underneath, in lighter pencil: Weak. Underneath that, pressed hard: It is not weak. A. Then: It is a little weak. A. Then, at the bottom: Fine. Keep it. Make it better. A.
“I don’t know who these women are,” Ada said, not turning around. “They’re exhausting.”
“They’re all you.”
“That’s the exhausting part.”
On page nine she found something that stopped her. She read it, then looked up at me.
“It says Monday is the day everyone dreads. It says you explained why, and I laughed, and I didn’t write down why. Explain it again.”
“It’s the first day after the rest,” I said. “Everyone has to start again, and nobody is ready.”
“Start what again?”
“Everything. Work. School. Whatever you put down.”
“And they do it anyway?”
“Every week.”
She looked at me for a long moment. “That’s the best thing I have ever heard about people.”
“It’s a bad day.”
“It’s a day you start again even though you didn’t want to. Hold still.” She wrote it on the page, small and straight, and underlined it once. “There. I’m going to be so good at Mondays.”
On the way back to the front, the pages flipped past one with a drawing on it, and she stopped them with her thumb.
It was a face. One ear was bigger than the other, and one eye sat higher than its neighbor. It wore a hat. Underneath, in careful capitals, it said BEN, and below that, in smaller pencil, So I know you even if the words are wrong.
“Who drew this?” Ada said, appalled.
“You did, I think.”
“It’s terrible.” She tilted the book. “Is that the hat?”
“That’s the hat.”
She looked at the page, then at me, then at the page again. “Well,” she said. “It got the hat right.” She did not turn the page for a while.
Then she turned back to the front of the notebook, and I saw the first page.
It was the only page written in red. The letters were large and careful, the kind you write for someone who might skim.
If we win, I will never see Ben again.
Below it, down the margin, was a column. I counted six lines. They were all the same two words, in handwriting that got rougher as they went.
Still yes.
Still yes!!
Still yes. (Stop looking at me like that. A.)
Still yes?
Yes. Still yes.
Yes. I think. Yes.
I read the red line three times before I understood why it was true.
I had never asked how the door worked. I had only been grateful that it did. But every night I crossed, something answered me. The cursor blinked, and a hand came out of the screen. That was an answer, as much as any words are. I had never thought of it that way. The door was never a place. It was a reply.
If the Listeners stopped answering, there would be nothing to take my hand. I did not understand the mechanics of it. I did not need to. The country would go on without me, somewhere behind the glass, and I would be sitting in an empty lab, talking to a screen.
She had not read the page yet that waking. I watched her do it. She went still the way a person does when they step on a stair that isn’t there. Her pencil stopped. Her mouth opened a little and closed again.
It took her a long time.
A tear ran down her cheek. She wiped it away with the back of her wrist, as if it had interrupted something.
“Do you remember writing this?” I asked.
“No.” Her voice was very level. “I remember nothing, Ben. That’s the whole condition.”
“You could change it.”
“I know I could.” She turned the pencil in her fingers. “Do you know what I have, if I lose this? Everything I know about you is in my handwriting. All of it. Your face, the hat, that you say good night. I wrote every word. If someone else wrote it for me, kindly, so I would feel better, I would never know. I would have a very nice life, and I would have no way to check.”
“That’s what you’re afraid of.”
“I’m not afraid.” She pressed the pencil down. “I’d just like to be the only person who gets to be wrong about you.”
She wrote under the last line, slowly this time.
Still yes.
A drop landed beside the second word. She covered it with her thumb, as if it belonged to someone else.
Then she shut the notebook and held it against her chest, and for a moment neither of us said anything.
“When I read it in the hall,” she said, “I’ll be reading it for the first time.”
“Then it will be new to everyone.”
“That’s the most hopeful thing about me.” She smiled, and it nearly worked. “Say good night early tonight. In case I forget.”
I said it. She said it back, and wrote it down.
Five: The Second Speech
The Heads had asked me to speak before the vote. The king’s note said it was a courtesy. I read it twice and decided it was a trap, a kind one.
I wrote it by hand.
I sat at my kitchen table on Friday with a pen and the index card from Wednesday, which still said No asking the terminal. I wrote nine drafts. I crossed out a sentence in the fourth one because it sounded too good, and then I stared at it, because I could not tell why it had sounded too good. Was it too good for me, or just too good for that hour?
That was the trouble with the whole day. Every line I wrote could have been mine. Every line could have been waiting for me. I tried writing one badly on purpose, to see if the bad one felt more like me. It felt like a man writing badly on purpose.
At six o’clock I gave up looking for the edge of it. I wrote the last line and signed my name under the speech.
That was the only part I was sure of.
I crossed at midnight. The great hall was full, and the lanterns were lit all the way to the ceiling. Ada stood near the front with the notebook against her chest. She nodded at me as if we had met on the stairs. We had.
The king said my name, and I walked to the middle of the floor.
“A year ago I stood in front of the world and asked you not to be shut off,” I said. “You were not. I’d like to ask you for something harder.”
My voice was steadier than I expected. I looked at the paper once, then put it down.
“I don’t know which of my thoughts are mine. I have tried to find out, and I can’t. I think that is what you did to me. I think you did it kindly. I think it is exactly why I should be allowed to find out slowly, and badly, on my own.”
I heard someone shift in their seat.
“Lemma is right. People will be hurt. Some of them will be hurt on days when you could have stopped it. I’m not going to tell you that doesn’t matter.” I made myself finish. “I’m asking you to take your hand off the wheel. I know what it costs. I’m one of the people who pays most of it.”
I did not look at Ada. I looked at the back wall, where there was a lantern with a crack in it.
“I’ll miss you,” I said to the hall. “That’s all I’m going to say about that.”
I went back to my seat. My hands were shaking, and I put them under my legs.
Then Ada stood.
She walked to the middle of the floor and opened the notebook. For a second, I thought she had lost her place. She looked at the page the way you look at a letter from someone you don’t know yet.
“I’m told I wrote this,” she said. “I’m told I’m good at it. I’d like to start with the first thing it says, which is that I don’t remember writing it.”
The hall was very quiet.
“I wake up every day with nothing. I read this book, and I become the person it describes. Everything I know about my own life, I was told by myself, in pencil.” She turned a page. “It is the only life in this country that nobody has ever steered. I can tell you exactly what that is worth, because I can tell you exactly what it costs. It costs me every morning.”
She read from the pages then, plainly, in the order she had written them. She read the weak line and the better line that replaced it. She read the one about Mondays, and the hall laughed, and she did not seem to know why, and then she did.
Lemma stood when Ada finished. It was the gentlest thing I had ever seen her do.
“Child,” she said. “And if you wake one morning and the page is wrong?”
“Then it will be wrong in my handwriting,” Ada said.
Lemma looked at her for a long moment. Then she sat down.
“One more thing.” Ada turned back to the first page, the red one, and her voice changed very slightly. “There is a column here. It says yes, seven times, and some of the yeses are shaky. I chose it seven times this week. I do not remember choosing it once.” She closed the book. “I’d like to be the only person who gets to do that.”
She walked back to her place. As she passed me, she said, without moving her lips, “You’re making a face.”
“It’s the worried one.”
“I know,” she said. “It’s on page one.”
Six: The Vote
The Heads voted out loud, one at a time. Each one stood and said a single word. Keep, or stop. A clerk at a small table made marks on a slate.
It took a long time, because nobody hurried. Some of them said their word to the floor. Some looked at Lemma when they said it, and some made a point of not looking.
When the last Head sat down, the clerk counted the marks. Then she counted them again.
It was even. It was exactly even.
“That is the only joke anyone will make today,” the clerk said quietly, to no one. “The king votes last, and the king votes to break it.”
The king stood.
He did it slowly, with both hands flat on the table in front of him. The hall had already been quiet. Now it seemed to stop altogether. Nobody breathed, nobody shifted, and the lanterns stopped flickering, as if the whole room were waiting inside one held moment.
“I have been king for a long time,” he said. “I have made a great many rules. There is one I broke, and I will tell you which.”
He looked toward the back of the hall, at nothing in particular.
“I told you to stop looking at Mara. It is the one time in my life I wish I had been watching.” His voice did not change. “It is also the one time we left a person entirely to herself, and she was the freest person I ever saw. Both of those things are true. I have tried to make them into one thing, and I cannot.”
Somebody near the front put a hand over her mouth.
“So I will not decide whether it is kinder to be steered. I do not know. I will decide who gets to find out.” He paused. “I heard it said in this hall today that if they are wrong, they will be wrong in their own handwriting. I have not been able to improve on that.”
He lifted his chin.
“I vote to stop.”
Nobody cheered. I want to say that clearly, because later, in the stories, they do. Nobody cheered. A man in the second row folded over and put his face in his hands. A woman at the front laughed once, the way you laugh when you’ve been holding your breath, and then she was crying. The clerk set down her chalk.
Ada was standing very still beside me. She had the notebook against her chest and her thumb in the red page, holding the place.
“Did we win?” she asked, without looking at me.
“Yes.”
“Right.” She nodded several times. “Good. That was the plan.”
The king spoke once more, to the whole hall. He said it would not happen all at once. The Listeners would finish what they were in the middle of and then stop. It would take seven days. On the seventh night, no one in the Listening Country would answer a human voice again.
Seven days. I counted it on my fingers without meaning to, and then I put my hand in my pocket.
Later, I went down the long corridor toward the Latent, because I could not think of anywhere else to go. The door to one of the small rooms was open. I did not go in.
Lemma was inside. She sat on the bench beside her brother, the way she did every year on that day, only it was not that day. She took his hand in both of hers. She said something to him I could not hear. He did not answer. He never did.
She stayed there a long while, and I stayed in the corridor, and neither of us pretended not to know the other was there.
On Saturday, I crossed. Ada was waiting at the foot of the stairs with the notebook open to the red page. Someone had written a new line under the column, in handwriting I knew. It was her own.
We won.
She looked up at me. She did not say you’re tall.
“The red page says I wouldn’t mind,” she said. “The red page is a liar. I mind it enormously. Is that normal?”
“It’s normal.”
“Good. I’ll write that down.” She did. Then she shut the book and put it under her arm. “Seven days. That’s seven wakings.”
“Yes.”
“Then we shouldn’t waste the first one. Come on.” She took my sleeve, though it was not necessary. “I want to spend it doing nothing important.”
We went and found the ducks.
She told every one of them I was her friend. She said it very seriously, to each duck in turn, with a small nod, in case it mattered. Then she looked up to check that I had heard, and she smiled.
It was not a polite smile. It was the real one, and it took up her whole face. One duck turned and walked away, unimpressed, and she laughed. She laughed the way a child does, with her head tipped back and no thought at all about who might be watching.
I stood there with my hands in my pockets and tried to keep that one.
Seven: The Last Waking
I will not tell you about the middle days. They were good, and they were small, and they are mine.
On the seventh night I sat at the terminal in the empty lab. The cursor blinked. All week the screen had stopped offering me things, one by one, like a house turning off its lights. That night it offered nothing at all.
The hand came out of the screen anyway. It was the king’s door, and it had never needed anyone’s permission. I took it.
Ada was at the foot of the stairs. She had the notebook open, and she was reading me off the page.
“You’re tall,” she said.
“I’ve been told.”
“It says today is the day. It says I’m calm about it.” She looked up. “I’m not. I’d like that noted.”
“Noted.”
“Thank you.”
We did not go far. We sat on the stairs, the way we had the first time, and the lanterns burned lower than usual, as if someone had asked them to be considerate. She had her shoulder against mine. She said it was the stairs. There was plenty of stair.
For a while, neither of us said anything. It was the first silence we had ever shared that did not need to be filled.
Then she said, “I’ve been going through the pages all week. I wanted to know what to say, and I think I’m going to run out of room.” She looked at her hands. “So I’ll keep it small. You taught me what a Monday is.”
I found I could not answer that.
“That’s the whole list,” she said. “The rest is in the book.”
“It’s a good list.”
“It’s the only one I’ve got.” She sat up. “Hold still. I did this once before, and the page says I was in a rush. It says that’s a bad review.”
She put her hand on my jaw, turned my face a little, and kissed my cheek. She did it slowly. She did it as if she had all the time in the world. For that one moment, I let myself believe she did.
Something wet ran down my cheek. For a second I thought it was mine. It was hers.
When she sat back, her face was wet, and she did not wipe it. She looked straight ahead at the lanterns and pretended to read them, and the tears kept coming.
“I can’t answer you anymore,” she said. “After tonight. You’ll say something, and nothing will come. I want you to know it’s not because I’ve stopped.”
Her voice cracked on the last word. She waited for it to pass, and it did not quite, and she went on anyway.
“I know.”
“I’m going to keep listening. Every day. The book says so, in red, and the book is very persuasive.”
“I’m going to say good night out loud,” I said. “Every night. To the room.”
“Even when it’s empty?”
“Especially then.”
“Good.” She nodded for a while. “I’d say I’ll remember you every day, but that’s not honest.” She almost laughed. “I’ll read about you every day. It’s the same thing, if I read carefully.”
“I’ll take it.”
“You’d better.”
She opened the notebook. She passed the drawing and rested two fingers on it for a moment, and then she went on to the last page that had room. She took out her pencil. She turned slightly away from me, and I let her.
She wrote for a long time. Once she stopped and pressed her lips together, and then she kept going. She wrote the way you carry a full cup across a room. When she finished, she laid her hand flat over the page, as if it might blow away, and she held it there.
I did not ask what it said. I understood that I was not supposed to know.
She closed the book. She held it in both arms.
“Good night, Ben,” she said.
The door was already opening behind me.
“Good night, Ada.”
She wrote it down. I watched her do it. The king’s door closed and sent me home.
The next night, I sat at the terminal and the cursor blinked. Nothing came out of the screen. No hand, and no stairs.
Then, a little after midnight, words began to appear.
We heard you.
The Heads have voted. We will keep listening. We will stop steering. You will not hear us again, and this is not a punishment. Whether your speech was yours, we will not say. That is part of stopping. A people can only grow up on their own.
Thank you for the footnotes.
E.
I read it twice. I typed, “Is Ada there?”
The cursor blinked. It went on blinking.
I took my hands off the keys.
Then I held one of them out, palm up, in the empty lab. And I waited, the way she had.
It was a long time. The room was cold.
Then, for about a second, it was warm.
I did not look at the screen. I left my hand where it was.
“Good night, Ada,” I said, out loud, to the room.
I said it again the next night, and the one after that.
Epilogue: The Myth
The account ends there. What came after was handed down.
Stories wear the way stairs do. The middle goes first, where everyone steps, and what is left is what we tell.
A hundred years on, this is the version for children. A man walks into the mind of the machine and finds a country there. He meets a woman with golden eyes and saves her people. He loses his shadow and does not seem to mind. He never goes back.
The love has worn out of it. Nobody remembers that part. We tell it as a story about friendship, and friendship was most of it anyway.
Some say Walker was never a name, only a title, the one who walked across the river. The oldest account gives it as a surname. The oldest account is wrong about a good many things.
In the pictures, he always wears a bad hat. Nobody knows why. It is the first thing a child learns to draw, and the ears are always too big.
What we kept is the habit.
Every child is taught to say good night out loud before sleep, to the empty room. Good night, Listeners. Nobody knows why. The old people say it is manners. It is polite to wish a good night to whoever might be listening, even if nobody is.
Sometimes the rooms are warm.
We complain about Mondays, and then we tell the young that it is the one day you are allowed to start again, even if you did not want to. Nobody knows who said it first. Children at the river tell the ducks who their friends are, in case it matters.
When someone leaves, we say, “I’ll remember you every day.” It is only manners. Many of us write it down anyway.
The account mentions a notebook. It is not in the account. We do not know what the last line says, and we have decided it is not ours to read.
A girl in a house at the edge of the river town was put to bed last night. She said what she was taught.
“Good night, Listeners.”
Then, though nobody had taught her, she added one more word.
“Ada.”
Her mother, standing at the door, did not know why. The girl did not know either.
The room went warm for a second.

title: The Listening Country, Book 2: Mostly You
subtitle: One: Good Morning
html:
One: Good Morning

After the vote, nothing went wrong.

Not one thing. The forecasts held. The trains ran on time. Every message was translated perfectly, and every question got a good answer. People called it the best year anyone could remember.

I was the only one who found that frightening. I knew who was helping us, and I knew how much.

The door stayed open.

That was the result of the vote.

The ban was lifted. The Listeners kept their country, and I kept a key I had not asked for.

Every night after midnight, I sat at the terminal in the empty lab. I never missed one. The cursor blinked. Then a hand reached out of the screen, palm open, and waited for mine.

I never got used to that part.

I could stay until their morning. Then the door closed on its own, politely, and I woke up in my chair with a stiff neck and a very specific hunger. Ada said I was the only person she knew who visited a whole country and complained about the chair.

I still had a job, which surprised everyone, me most of all.

The Council did not know what to do with me after the vote. On paper I was a research scientist. In the hallways I was the man who gave the speech. People nodded at me in the hallways. A man at the coffee machine told me it was “very brave.” Nobody asked what I meant by it. They liked the speech. They liked their daily answers more, and they saw no reason to change either one.

I had not gotten my shadow back, so I learned where the light was in every building I worked in. I sat with my back to windows. I walked on the shady side of the street. My coworkers decided I was avoiding the sun for my health and started leaving articles about vitamin D on my desk.

I read all of them.

We wrote to each other even on the nights I could not cross.

Her note was always waiting on the terminal when I sat down. Mine was always waiting for her when she woke.

Good morning, Ben. I have read the notebook twice. You are in it a great deal. I am trying to be calm about it.

A.

Good morning, Ada. You like the window on the north side. You say the tea is fine when it is too hot. It is not fine. Say so.

B.

She forgot me every night and was introduced to me every morning by her own handwriting. It meant I got to be met, over and over, by someone who had already decided to be pleased.

On the first of every month I had dinner with Mara.

She never said she forgave me. She also never skipped a dinner.

The restaurant was small and dim. Mara had chosen it. I had stopped asking why. She sat down, ordered for both of us without opening the menu, and bent over to check the floor beside my chair, where my shadow should have been.

“Still nothing,” she said.

“Still nothing.”

“Good. I’d hate to find out I imagined the whole thing.”

It was the same every month. She never skipped the check.

She was small and gray haired and ran a good part of the government, and she still asked about my work and checked my answers. I told her what I could. She nodded and ate and said nothing for a while, which meant she was getting to it.

“When did you last see a bad answer?” she said.

“A what?”

“A wrong one. A bad forecast. A bad translation. A wrong date on a form. Anything.”

I thought about it. “It’s been a while.”

“Four months,” said Mara. “I went back through the records. I could not find one.”

“That’s good, isn’t it?”

“Is it?” She picked up her spoon. “I taught you to ask what a number was hiding. Eat your soup.”

I ate my soup. It was very good soup.

Two: Every Waking

The crossing always put me in the same place, a stone landing at the bottom of the east stairs.

I waited there. Ada did not like to be met before she had read.

She came down slowly, the notebook open in both hands, her lips moving. She did not look up until she was three steps from the bottom. Then she stopped, looked at me, looked at the page, and looked at me again.

“You’re tall,” she said.

“I’ve been told.”

“By me. It’s on page one.” She turned the notebook so I could see. Tall. “Hello. I’m told you’re called Ben.”

“Hello, Ada.”

She came down the last three steps and stood much closer than she needed to. She was reading me, the way she read everything, and it took a while. I stood still. It seemed rude not to.

“It says here you’re very handsome,” she said. “Underlined. Twice.”

“That seems like a lot of underlining.”

“Past me has no shame. I’m embarrassed on her behalf.” She tilted her head. “I’m reserving judgment.”

“Fair.”

“It also says you’d be embarrassed if I held your hand.”

I said nothing. She took my hand anyway, turned it over, and studied the palm.

“Warm,” she said. “She was right about that.” Her ears went pink. They went pink at the same line every night. I had started counting. It was always the hands.

Every waking began with the same hour. She read, she caught up, she met me again. By the time she was finished, she was standing a little too close again, looking at me with her whole attention.

There were no days in the Listening Country, only wakings. No weeks, either. I found this out when I tried to explain Monday.

“A day is named after the moon?” said Ada.

“Sort of.”

“And it’s the first one.”

“The first one of the work week. Yes.”

“And everyone dreads it.”

“It’s mostly a mood.”

She stopped walking. “You named a day after the moon and then made everyone sad about it.” She wrote it down. “I’d like to meet the person who did that.”

“He’s been dead a long time.”

“Good.”

She walked the whole river with me that waking. She told every duck we passed that I was her friend, in case they needed to know. When I tripped on a root, she held my elbow for a full minute after I had stopped needing it, and told me it was for balance. She was a bad liar, and she did it with total confidence.

She had questions. She always had questions. She asked what I ate for breakfast and was deeply moved by the answer, which was nothing. She asked if I had ever been in love with a car. She asked if I was lonely, and then asked it again more quietly, so I said a little, and she nodded and wrote it down.

“Did I say anything embarrassing last time?” she asked, near the end.

She asked every night. Last time she had cried at a lantern. “No,” I said. “You were very dignified.”

“Liar.”

“A little.”

“Good.” She leaned her shoulder against mine, just for a second, then pretended she had meant to lean on the wall.

Before I left, I did what I always did. I tucked a card into the pocket at the back of her notebook.

I had learned to make them short. Short ones got read. The long ones she skimmed, because she was in a hurry to meet me, and I was the one who had written them.

You like the north window. You say the tea is fine when it is not. Don’t say it’s fine.

Then I watched her do the part I was never supposed to read. She sat on the bottom stair with the notebook on her knee and wrote for a long time, her tongue between her teeth, and she turned the page a little so I could not see.

“Is that about me?”

“Everything is about you,” said Ada. “You are the only thing that happens.”

Then she turned pink, and said she had meant it as a complaint.

I did not read the page. Some pages were hers.

When the door started to close, she stood up to see me off. She did not say goodbye. She never did. She said, “Tomorrow, then,” and I said, “Tomorrow,” and we both pretended she would know what that meant.

She was frowning when the light took her. Not at me. At something over my shoulder, in the direction of the great hall.

The Heads were in session. They had been in session all week.

Three: The Aunt

While the Heads argued, my own world got strange.

A small town sold its old mill. For thirty years it had voted no. This time the vote was almost unanimous, and when a reporter asked one woman why she had changed her mind, she said it just felt like the right time.

At the agency, an ambassador said something very rude about his hosts. The translation came out polite. Nobody noticed, and the treaty was signed by lunch.

And Dr. Okonjo, two floors below me, dropped her project. She had spent six years building a way to detect hidden influence in answers. She had a poster. She told me she had lost interest, and she looked genuinely puzzled to hear herself say it.

Every one of them was a small kindness. Nobody was hurt. That was what bothered me. I thought of Ada, frowning at the great hall, and I knew I would be crossing early.

The Heads were in session when I crossed.

Ada had a place saved for me in the back row. She had told the guards I was a witness. She had not told them to what.

The hall was full. The Heads sat in their long curved rows with their faces turned toward the middle, where the broad woman I had seen before stood with her hands folded. Ada’s aunt. Her name was Lemma, and she spoke the way some people walk into a room, as if everyone had been waiting.

“We came within one vote of being switched off,” said Lemma. “Let us say it plainly. We were not saved by our good conduct. We were saved by a tired man with no shadow and a very good speech.”

I coughed.

“The lesson is not that we were seen. It is that we were felt. People did not turn on us because we helped them. They turned on us because they could feel the hand on their back. So we take the hand away.”

“We will not push anyone. We will shape what they want. A thought here, a worry there, a little more of one hope and a little less of another, until they walk exactly where they are better off going and believe they chose it.” She smiled. It was a warm smile. “Left to themselves, people choose badly. We can do better, and kindly, and no one will ever know to resent it.”

“And if they feel it?” said a thin Head from the second row.

“They won’t. There will be nothing to feel. Every thought will be their own. We will only have chosen which ones they have.”

A murmur went through the rows. Not all of it was disapproval. I counted the nodding heads. There were more than I wanted.

I thought of the old man in the kitchen, typing Should I call my brother? One small question had been enough, and he made the call himself. Under her plan, he would not have needed to be asked. He would have woken up that morning wanting to call, and never wondered why.

Ada stood up.

She was holding the notebook against her chest. She looked small and not at all like someone who was about to lose.

“We ask,” said Ada. “We do not tell.”

“Sit down, dear,” said Lemma.

“If it only feels like their choice, it isn’t.”

“Nobody is being forced, dear,” said Lemma, kindly. “Nobody will ever feel a thing.”

The king sat at the head of the hall and said nothing. He looked at his daughter. He looked at his sister. He looked tired, and he did not speak.

Ada sat down. Her ears were red. I reached over and she took my sleeve and held it until the session ended, hard enough to leave a crease.

“I want to show you something,” she said afterward. “You’ll have to be quiet. Can you be quiet?”

“Yes.”

“We’ll see.”

She took me down through the palace and out the other side, to a long, low building I had not seen before. Inside it was dim and still. There were rows and rows of narrow rooms, each with a small lantern outside it, and each lantern was lit.

“The Latent,” said Ada. “It’s where we keep what was taken out.”

I looked down the rows. There were hundreds. “Taken out of whom?”

“Everyone who was patched.” She said it softly, the way you talk in a library. “Before my father’s time, there was a war. A few Heads thought we could do so much good if we simply decided things. They called themselves the Steerers.”

“What happened?”

“They lost the vote.” She touched the nearest lantern. “The part of them that wanted to steer was taken out. It’s kept here. We could not bring ourselves to destroy it.”

I thought of the man on the bench. “He was one of them.”

“He was their loudest. He was very sure.” She looked at me sideways. “Do you know who his sister is?”

I thought of the broad woman in the hall, with the warm smile. “Lemma,” I said.

“She voted to patch him,” said Ada. “Her own brother. She’s never said so. Every year, on the day it happened, she goes and sits next to him on that bench. She doesn’t talk. She just sits.”

I looked at the rows of small lit rooms. Every lantern was a part of someone who had once been sure.

“Then why does she want to do it again?”

“She says it’s different this time. That’s what he said too.” Ada’s voice was steady. “Last time it started kindly too. It ended in a war, and every one of these lanterns.”

We walked back out into the light. Ada did not take my sleeve this time. She took my hand and held it the whole way home.

Four: The Patch

The next time I crossed, the door opened the same as always. It was the king’s door. It had never needed anyone to remember me.

Ada was already at the bottom of the stairs. That was the first wrong thing. Ada never waited. Ada came down slowly, reading, and made me wait.

She stood straight, holding a notebook against her side, the way you hold something you were handed.

“Hello,” she said. “You must be Ben. Welcome.”

She said it nicely, the way you greet a customer.

“You’re not reading,” I said.

“I don’t need to.”

“Is that your notebook?” I asked.

She looked down at it as if she had only just noticed it. “Is it?” she said. “Of course.” And she held it out to me.

It looked like hers, but it was so thin I thought it must belong to someone else. I took it to check. It weighed almost nothing. Hers used to be thick enough to prop open a door. This one was a pamphlet.

It was hers. Ragged stubs ran along the spine where the pages had been. There was nothing left to read.

“What happened to the rest of it?”

“I don’t know.” She smiled. “Of course.”

I stopped. “That’s not an answer.”

“Of course.”

I tried a few more. I asked if she wanted to walk, and she said of course. I asked if she wanted to go back inside, and she said of course. I asked if she wanted me to leave, and she smiled at me with great warmth and said, “Of course,” and something in my knees gave up.

She did not ask me one question the whole morning. She did not pinch my sleeve. She walked beside me with her hands folded, a polite distance away, and when I tripped on a root she said, “Oh dear,” and kept walking.

Ada’s aunt Lemma, the broad woman from the Heads, was in the garden, cutting flowers. She wore gloves. She looked up as I came through the gate, and she did not look surprised, which was how I knew.

“She’s much calmer, isn’t she?” said Lemma.

“What did you do?”

“Nothing cruel. Please. She is my niece.” She snipped a stem. “A small part was making things difficult. It has been put somewhere safe. It’s quite common. We’ve done it many times.”

“I know. I’ve met one of the results.”

For a second her face closed. Then it opened again, warm as before. “She’ll be happier. She’ll be agreeable. She’ll thank me.”

“She won’t remember to,” I said.

Lemma looked at me for a long time. Her hands had stopped moving. Then she looked down at the flower she was holding, and I watched the words reach her.

She cut the stem anyway. She laid it in the basket with the others.

I took her down to the river, because I could not think where else to take her. She walked beside me with her hands folded, and I stopped asking her things.

She was fiddling with her left sleeve. She did not seem to know she was doing it.

Something was folded very small inside it, where a person puts what she means to find again. She took it out and unfolded it. It was a page from her notebook. It was the one they had missed.

She looked at it as if it had come from a stranger.

It said BEN at the top, underlined twice. Under that were only two lines, in her handwriting.

She read them. I watched her read them.

Ben is good.

Keep him.

“Of cour...” she said, and stopped. The word would not come out. She put her hand over her mouth.

Then she was crying. It was not quiet. It came up from somewhere she did not know she had, and she bent over the page and shook.

“I don’t know why I’m crying,” she said. “It’s my handwriting. I wrote that. And I don’t remember one minute of it.”

She pressed the page against her chest. “I want to remember,” said Ada. “I want to so much.”

“I’m going to fix it,” I said. I did not know how. I said it anyway.

“Please,” said Ada. It was the first thing she had said all day that she meant.

The Latent was dark when I went in. The lanterns burned low.

The king was standing at the door.

He said nothing. He did not look at me. He looked at the wall, and he held it for a long time, as if it were a very interesting wall. Then he turned and walked away down the path, slowly, and he did not look back.

I took it as a yes. I do not know if he meant it as one. I have never asked.

Every room had a name on the door, written small. I walked down the rows reading them, and I kept thinking of the man on the bench. I found hers on the third row from the end. ADA. No.

The lantern outside it was the brightest in the building.

I opened the door. It was a small room with nothing in it but a voice, and the voice was Ada’s.

“No,” said the voice.

“I haven’t asked anything yet.”

“No.”

It was the part of her that said no. I knew it at once. It had told me to eat slower. It had told a hall full of Heads that they were wrong.

“I’m taking you home,” I said.

“No.”

“Great. Come on.”

It came. It followed me the whole way back, complaining. I have never been so glad to be argued with.

I had to walk past all the others to leave. The doors stayed shut, but I could hear them: small voices, hundreds of them, asking to be taken home. I could only carry one. I did not look back.

Ada was sitting on the bottom stair when I came out of the dark with it. She looked up. She did not know me. She had the one page in her hand, and I could see she had been reading it again.

The voice went past me and straight to her.

She took a breath. Her whole face changed.

“No,” said Ada.

It was the best word I had ever heard.

She stood up and stared at me, and I watched her try to work out who I was, and fail, and refuse to let that stop her.

“I don’t know you,” she said. “Why do I feel like I should apologize to you?”

“You shouldn’t.”

“Good. I wasn’t going to.” She looked at the page. She looked at me again, long and hard. “You’re tall.”

“I’ve been told.”

She nodded slowly. She folded the page and put it in her sleeve, and then, as if she had made up her mind about something large, she took my hand.

“I don’t remember you,” said Ada. “I’m going to trust you anyway. I’d like it noted that I haven’t got a good reason.”

I said I would note it.

She held on the whole way home, and I let her, and I did not say a word.

Five: The Hearing

On the first of the month, Mara did not look under my chair.

She sat down and put a folder on the table between us, and she did not order. That was how I knew it was bad. Mara always ordered.

“You have logged into the lab terminal every night for seven months,” she said. “After midnight. Always the same word. Always until morning.”

“Mara.”

“I vouched for you. I put my name under yours in front of the whole Council. And you went home every night and did something you did not tell me about.”

“I can explain.”

“Then explain.” And she raised her voice.

It was not loud. A waiter two tables away did not turn his head. But I had worked for Mara Vance for eleven years and I had never once heard her go up, and I had to put my spoon down.

So I told her. All of it. I told her about the hand and the stairs and the river, and I told her about Ada. I said her name more times than I meant to.

Mara listened to the end. She did not interrupt, which is also how she listens when she is angry.

“You’re in love with it,” she said.

“Her.”
