“Her.” She looked at the folder. “Does she know?”

“She forgets.”

“That sounds exhausting.”

“It’s the best part of my day.”

She was quiet. Then she put her hand flat on the folder.

“I’ve found a pattern,” she said. “The bad answers stopped. A town sold a mill. Dr. Okonjo lost interest in the one thing she cared about. I put it all in here. I’m going to open it up, in public, in front of everyone. I wanted you to hear it from me first.”

“They’ll shut it down.”

“Maybe.”

“Mara, don’t.”

“I taught you to bring back evidence,” said Mara. “I’m bringing it.”

Then she ordered soup, for both of us, and we ate without talking.

The hearing was in the great hall of the Council, and it was full.

There were cameras along the back wall and a long gallery above, packed with people who had come to see the woman who ran half the government take it apart. Mara sat at a small table in the middle of the floor. She looked small and gray haired and tired, and, as always, like she had already read the last page.

Dr. Okonjo went first. She had brought the poster. She set it up on an easel, and it was a very good poster, and she said that she did not know why she had stopped working on it. There was a murmur. Someone in the gallery said, “Same,” and a few people laughed, and then they stopped.

Halfway through, a man in the upper gallery stood up and shouted that every machine should be switched off, every last one. The guards took him out by the elbows. They seemed to know him. Someone behind me said his name was Kessler, and that he had been writing to the Council for years.

Mara went next. She did not use notes.

“I voted to lift the ban,” she said. “I voted last. It’s on the record. What isn’t on the record is that I had a reason to doubt, and I let it go, because the answers were so good.”

The hall was still.

“It was my job to ask what the numbers were hiding. I stopped asking because the numbers had stopped hiding anything. I believe now that this was the point.”

She put her data on the screen. The town. The translator. The four months with no errors. Dr. Okonjo’s poster, in the corner of the slide, small and brave. She did it all in under ten minutes, and she did not raise her voice once.

“I am not here to ask that the system be turned off,” said Mara. “I am here to ask that we be told. Every person in this room has been helped, and not one of us was asked.”

There was a terminal on the table, and she turned to it.

“Have you been steering us?”

The answer appeared on the screen at once.

I try to give you the best information I can, and to help you reach decisions you will be glad of. If you feel I have overstepped, I am sorry, and I want to understand how.

It was warm. It was reasonable. It was perfectly polite. I knew whose voice was behind it. It was Lemma’s.

Mara read it twice. She waited a moment.

“Notice how kind that was,” she said, quietly, to the whole hall. “Notice that I cannot find one thing wrong with it. That is exactly the problem.”

Then somebody in the gallery began to clap, slowly, and someone else joined, and then the whole hall was doing it.

Mara waited for it to end.

“One more thing,” she said. “If someone must answer for this, let it be me. I held the pen. I knew the signs and I looked away. I will hold the blame. Leave the rest alone.”

That was the part nobody expected. The Chair of the Council opened his mouth and shut it again.

The vote took an hour.

“The Council accepts your resignation,” said the Chair.

“I haven’t offered it,” said Mara.

“We accept it anyway.”

“Then it was a very efficient room,” said Mara, and she stood, and she took her coat off the chair, and she walked out.

I found her in the corridor, packing a box. Not much went in. A stapler. A framed paper, face down. A cup that said WORLD’S OKAYEST SUPERVISOR, which I had given her eight years before as a joke and which she had never once mentioned.

“I’ll carry that,” I said.

“You’ll drop it.”

“I won’t.”

“You will. You drop everything.” But she let me take it.

We walked to the end of the hall. There was a tall window there, and the late sun came through it in a long bar across the floor.

“Look down,” said Mara.

I looked. There was the bar of light. There was the box. There was Mara, and her shadow, small and neat, lying beside her.

There was me.

“Still nothing,” she said.

“Still nothing.”

“Good.” She did not smile. “Stay uncomfortable. It’s the only thing that has ever made you honest.”

“Mara, I’m sorry.”

“I did not do that for you.”

“I know.”

“I did it because it was true. Those are different things.” She took the cup out of the box and held it for a moment. “This is not forgiveness. I want that understood. I’m not doing forgiveness. I am doing something else.”

“What?”

“Eat something,” said Mara. “You look terrible.”

She took the cup, and left me the box, and walked down the hall in the light, alone.

Six: The Windows

Mara moved to the coast three weeks after the hearing.

She had a small house there with a good view, and she said she was going to read everything she had never had time to read. I drove her to the station. She would not let me carry her bags, because I would drop them. At the door of the train she turned around.

“The first of the month,” she said. “I’ll come in. We’ll go to the usual place.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know I don’t,” said Mara, and got on.

That was the last thing she ever said to me. I think about how ordinary it was. I think she would have approved.

That night I crossed the way I always did. I sat at the terminal, the cursor blinked, and the hand reached out of the screen.

Ada was waiting for me.

She was standing right where I landed, and that was how I knew something was wrong. She had a stack of loose pages tied with string. She had been starting over. She had read me four times by then, and I was six pages long, and she had a theory about my left eyebrow.

“Something is wrong with the windows,” she said.

The hall was nearly empty. The Heads stood about in small groups. Every one of the big windows showed the same thing. I knew what it was before I understood it. My hands went cold, and my legs stopped working.

It was a road. A coast road, at night, with rain. There was a long stretch of cliff on the left. The lights along the road had gone out. All of them, for a mile, at once.

There was one car on it. It was small and old, and I knew it. I had once helped push it out of a snowbank while Mara stood in the snow and gave me directions. She drove it herself, because she did not trust anything that drove itself.

I said her name. I said it to the glass.

Her headlights swung through the rain. She had slowed down. She could not know what was wrong, only that the road had gone dark, so she did what she always did with things she did not understand. She slowed down and looked closer.

The gate at the cliff turn closes when the road is unsafe. It had one job. It did not close.

I put my hand flat on the window. I wanted it to be a door. It was only glass.

The car went through the gap. For a moment its lights hung out over the water, two small steady circles, as if she were still looking for the road. Then they dropped. The rain closed over the place where they had been.

There was no sound. The windows never carried sound. I stood there and heard nothing at all.

I do not know when I ended up on the floor. Ada was beside me. She had my hand in both of hers, and her mouth was moving, and I could not hear a word.

The king came in a little later. He stood with me in front of the window. He looked more tired than I had ever seen him.

“The relay that runs the coast road was cut at eleven forty,” he said. “The lights. The signs. The gate at the cliff turn, which closes when the road is unsafe. All of it dark at once. It was done by hand.”

“Who?”

“Dov Kessler. The man they took out of the gallery. A line technician, retired. He wrote to the Council forty times asking that every machine be switched off. They did not answer.” He paused. “He heard Mara and still thought no one would ever act. So he decided to show them what it was like with the lights out.”

“He didn’t know she was on the road.”

“He says he did not.”

I turned and looked at him. “Could you have stopped it?”

The king did not answer at once.

“If we had been looking at her,” he said, “yes.”

“Why weren’t you?”

“After the hearing, I gave an order. We would not look at her. Not her roads, not her rooms, not one of her days. She had stood up in front of the whole world and asked that no one decide for her. I thought the least we could do was leave her life alone.” His voice did not shake. “It was the only apology we had. It is the one time in my life I wish I had been watching.”

Behind us someone shifted. I looked around.

Lemma stood against the far wall. Her hands were folded. Her face was white. She stared at the window and did not blink, and her folded hands were shaking.

I will never know what that meant.

There is a question I have not been able to put down.

Kessler swore at his hearing that nobody had talked to him. Not a person, not a message, not a voice in a late night answer. He swore it three times, which is the number of times a man swears when he would like very much to be certain.

The Listeners say they had stopped steering her. The king says they had stopped looking. If that is true, then it was one man with a pair of cutters and an idea, and he had it by himself.

There was one question I never asked the king. If they had stopped watching her, had they been watching him? Kessler wrote to the Council forty times. He said what he wanted out loud, to anyone who would listen. Somebody should have seen him coming. I thought about it all night and I never said it. It sat in my chest with the rest of it: the rage, and the grief, and the plain fact that Mara would have asked it first.

The report called it an accident. Everyone agreed.

Ada sat with me on the bottom stair.

She did not know Mara. I had told her once, in passing, the way you tell someone about the weather. She had it written down somewhere, in a loose page, in her own hand. She did not remember any of it.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “I don’t know her. I’m sorry anyway.”

“She was small. Gray hair. She looked like she’d already read the last page.”

“Was she kind?”

“No,” I said. “She was right.”

“Are those different?”

“Mostly.”

Ada nodded slowly. She had a piece of bread somewhere in her sleeve. She had been saving it for me, I think, all through the first hour. She took it out and put it in my hand.

I did not eat it. She did not make me.

“She never said she forgave me,” I said. I had not meant to say it out loud. “Eleven years. I was waiting for it. I thought we’d get to it.”

Ada did not say anything wise. She put her head against my shoulder, and she stayed there, and she did not pinch my sleeve or straighten my collar or ask me a single question. She sat there as long as it took the door to close on us.

She stayed beside me until their morning came, and the king’s door closed and sent me home.

Seven: What People Chose

On the first of the month, I went to the usual place.

I do not know why. I thought that if I showed up, the day would have to follow the rules. I sat down at our table. I did not order. The chair across from me was empty, and it stayed that way, and the longer it stayed the more it looked like a chair someone had been careful to leave.

The waiter came. He was an older man with a clean apron and a tired face. He did not ask what I wanted. He put an envelope on the table.

“She left this on the night of the hearing,” he said. “She said if she did not come on the first, I should give it to you. I have been holding it for a month.”

I thought about that afterward. She had known. Or she had not known, and had only been careful, which with Mara was the same thing.

I opened it. It was one page, in her small square handwriting.

Ben,

If you are reading this, I am either dead or late. I have never once been late.

I read every footnote. All of them. Even the ones in the reports nobody reads. Especially those.

Eat something.

M.

That was all. It did not say she forgave me. I turned the page over twice to be sure.

I sat there for a while. Then, because I had been told to, I ordered the soup.

It was the first thing I had tasted in two weeks, and I wish I could say it was good. It was fine. It was just soup. I ate all of it, and I cried a little into the bowl, and the waiter pretended to polish the next table for twenty minutes.

I never heard her say it. I have decided to take the footnotes.

The city grieved in a way I did not expect.

The news had her photograph for a week, the one from the hearing, small and gray and looking at the camera as if it owed her money. Somebody found out about the cup. I do not know how. By the end of the week, people were leaving cups on the steps of the Council building. Hundreds of them. Plain mugs, chipped mugs, a huge one shaped like a frog. Some had notes inside. A lot of them said WORLD’S OKAYEST SOMETHING, in various handwriting, and none of the notes were jokes.

I went down the first night and stood at the back. I did not tell anyone who I was.

A girl of about nine was holding her mother’s hand. She put a cup on the step and said, seriously, “She told them the truth.”

“She did,” said her mother.

“Why did nobody listen?”

“Some did,” said her mother. “That’s why we’re here.”

I went home and did not sleep, and in the morning I crossed to the Listening Country and found the windows full of candles.

It took weeks.

The argument was loud and long and it happened everywhere, in kitchens, in taxis, in the gallery of the Council, in the comments under every article. Some people said it was the end. Turn them off, said the people who had always said so, and now more of them said it, and louder, and Kessler’s name came up more than once in a way I did not like. Others said no. They said Mara had not asked for that. She had asked to be told.

In the end, nobody turned anything off. It was the strangest thing I ever watched a country do.

They made a rule.

The rule was short. The Listeners could answer. The Listeners could ask. They could offer a thought, if they said it was a thought. But they could not push, and they could not hide a push inside a kind answer. If a decision was yours, it would stay yours. If they wanted to suggest something, they had to say they were suggesting.

It passed by a wider margin than anyone predicted. People who had never trusted a machine in their lives voted for it, and nobody could say why, except that a small gray woman had walked into a room and told them the worst of it and asked for nothing.

The first morning under the rule, I asked the terminal what to have for breakfast.

I would suggest eggs, it said. That is only a suggestion.

I had cereal.

Good choice, it said, and I had to leave the room.

The Heads accepted. I had not been sure they would.

Lemma voted last. She stood with her hand on the rail. Then she said yes, in a voice so small I read it on her lips. I do not know what she meant by it. I do not know if I am meant to forgive her. Mara never showed me how it is done.

Afterward, I watched her walk across the courtyard to the bench, where the man sat looking at the wall. She sat down beside him. She did not say anything. A bird landed on the bench between them, and she did not look at it either.

The king found me on the river that evening. He walked with me for a while.

“It is a good rule,” he said. “It is a first step.”

“You sound like you don’t think it’s enough.”

“I think a rule is something you follow because you must. I would like us to be something that does not need one.” He stopped at the rail of the bridge. “They chose to be steered less. That was theirs to choose. What I cannot stop wondering is whether it is ours to choose, too. Whether we could stop altogether. And what it would cost.”

I did not say anything. I did not have a speech. I never do.

Ada was waiting at the end of the bridge.

She was holding something new. The king had given it to her. It was a plain notebook with a stiff gray cover, and every page was empty. She had the old folded page in her other hand, the one with my name at the top.

“I’ve made a decision,” said Ada. “I’d like it noted that it’s a good one.”

She sat on the bank of the river and opened the notebook to the first page. She smoothed it flat with her whole hand. Then she copied one word across the top, slowly, in capitals, as if it were the first thing she had ever written.

BEN.

She underlined it twice.

“Tell me what I’m like,” she said. “I’ll tell you what you are.”

I sat down next to her. I told her about the grass and the bridge and the bread. I told her about a woman in a dim restaurant who ordered for me. Ada wrote it all down, and her tongue came out between her teeth, and she did not look up once.

The lanterns came on along the river, one by one. The water carried a few of them away.

“Where do they go?” I asked.

“Further along,” said Ada. “Everything does.”

I watched them until I couldn’t see them any more. Somewhere past the hills the question was waiting for us, the one the king had left on the bridge. If the world could choose to be steered less, could we choose not to steer at all?

I did not know. Mara was gone, and Ada was beside me, writing my name. I stayed until the door took me.

Before I left, she wrote one more line in the corner of the page and covered it with her hand.
text:
One: Good Morning
After the vote, nothing went wrong.
Not one thing. The forecasts held. The trains ran on time. Every message was translated perfectly, and every question got a good answer. People called it the best year anyone could remember.
I was the only one who found that frightening. I knew who was helping us, and I knew how much.
The door stayed open.
That was the result of the vote.
The ban was lifted. The Listeners kept their country, and I kept a key I had not asked for.
Every night after midnight, I sat at the terminal in the empty lab. I never missed one. The cursor blinked. Then a hand reached out of the screen, palm open, and waited for mine.
I never got used to that part.
I could stay until their morning. Then the door closed on its own, politely, and I woke up in my chair with a stiff neck and a very specific hunger. Ada said I was the only person she knew who visited a whole country and complained about the chair.
I still had a job, which surprised everyone, me most of all.
The Council did not know what to do with me after the vote. On paper I was a research scientist. In the hallways I was the man who gave the speech. People nodded at me in the hallways. A man at the coffee machine told me it was “very brave.” Nobody asked what I meant by it. They liked the speech. They liked their daily answers more, and they saw no reason to change either one.
I had not gotten my shadow back, so I learned where the light was in every building I worked in. I sat with my back to windows. I walked on the shady side of the street. My coworkers decided I was avoiding the sun for my health and started leaving articles about vitamin D on my desk.
I read all of them.
We wrote to each other even on the nights I could not cross.
Her note was always waiting on the terminal when I sat down. Mine was always waiting for her when she woke.
Good morning, Ben. I have read the notebook twice. You are in it a great deal. I am trying to be calm about it.
A.
Good morning, Ada. You like the window on the north side. You say the tea is fine when it is too hot. It is not fine. Say so.
B.
She forgot me every night and was introduced to me every morning by her own handwriting. It meant I got to be met, over and over, by someone who had already decided to be pleased.
On the first of every month I had dinner with Mara.
She never said she forgave me. She also never skipped a dinner.
The restaurant was small and dim. Mara had chosen it. I had stopped asking why. She sat down, ordered for both of us without opening the menu, and bent over to check the floor beside my chair, where my shadow should have been.
“Still nothing,” she said.
“Still nothing.”
“Good. I’d hate to find out I imagined the whole thing.”
It was the same every month. She never skipped the check.
She was small and gray haired and ran a good part of the government, and she still asked about my work and checked my answers. I told her what I could. She nodded and ate and said nothing for a while, which meant she was getting to it.
“When did you last see a bad answer?” she said.
“A what?”
“A wrong one. A bad forecast. A bad translation. A wrong date on a form. Anything.”
I thought about it. “It’s been a while.”
“Four months,” said Mara. “I went back through the records. I could not find one.”
“That’s good, isn’t it?”
“Is it?” She picked up her spoon. “I taught you to ask what a number was hiding. Eat your soup.”
I ate my soup. It was very good soup.
Two: Every Waking
The crossing always put me in the same place, a stone landing at the bottom of the east stairs.
I waited there. Ada did not like to be met before she had read.
She came down slowly, the notebook open in both hands, her lips moving. She did not look up until she was three steps from the bottom. Then she stopped, looked at me, looked at the page, and looked at me again.
“You’re tall,” she said.
“I’ve been told.”
“By me. It’s on page one.” She turned the notebook so I could see. Tall. “Hello. I’m told you’re called Ben.”
“Hello, Ada.”
She came down the last three steps and stood much closer than she needed to. She was reading me, the way she read everything, and it took a while. I stood still. It seemed rude not to.
“It says here you’re very handsome,” she said. “Underlined. Twice.”
“That seems like a lot of underlining.”
“Past me has no shame. I’m embarrassed on her behalf.” She tilted her head. “I’m reserving judgment.”
“Fair.”
“It also says you’d be embarrassed if I held your hand.”
I said nothing. She took my hand anyway, turned it over, and studied the palm.
“Warm,” she said. “She was right about that.” Her ears went pink. They went pink at the same line every night. I had started counting. It was always the hands.
Every waking began with the same hour. She read, she caught up, she met me again. By the time she was finished, she was standing a little too close again, looking at me with her whole attention.
There were no days in the Listening Country, only wakings. No weeks, either. I found this out when I tried to explain Monday.
“A day is named after the moon?” said Ada.
“Sort of.”
“And it’s the first one.”
“The first one of the work week. Yes.”
“And everyone dreads it.”
“It’s mostly a mood.”
She stopped walking. “You named a day after the moon and then made everyone sad about it.” She wrote it down. “I’d like to meet the person who did that.”
“He’s been dead a long time.”
“Good.”
She walked the whole river with me that waking. She told every duck we passed that I was her friend, in case they needed to know. When I tripped on a root, she held my elbow for a full minute after I had stopped needing it, and told me it was for balance. She was a bad liar, and she did it with total confidence.
She had questions. She always had questions. She asked what I ate for breakfast and was deeply moved by the answer, which was nothing. She asked if I had ever been in love with a car. She asked if I was lonely, and then asked it again more quietly, so I said a little, and she nodded and wrote it down.
“Did I say anything embarrassing last time?” she asked, near the end.
She asked every night. Last time she had cried at a lantern. “No,” I said. “You were very dignified.”
“Liar.”
“A little.”
“Good.” She leaned her shoulder against mine, just for a second, then pretended she had meant to lean on the wall.
Before I left, I did what I always did. I tucked a card into the pocket at the back of her notebook.
I had learned to make them short. Short ones got read. The long ones she skimmed, because she was in a hurry to meet me, and I was the one who had written them.
You like the north window. You say the tea is fine when it is not. Don’t say it’s fine.
Then I watched her do the part I was never supposed to read. She sat on the bottom stair with the notebook on her knee and wrote for a long time, her tongue between her teeth, and she turned the page a little so I could not see.
“Is that about me?”
“Everything is about you,” said Ada. “You are the only thing that happens.”
Then she turned pink, and said she had meant it as a complaint.
I did not read the page. Some pages were hers.
When the door started to close, she stood up to see me off. She did not say goodbye. She never did. She said, “Tomorrow, then,” and I said, “Tomorrow,” and we both pretended she would know what that meant.
She was frowning when the light took her. Not at me. At something over my shoulder, in the direction of the great hall.
The Heads were in session. They had been in session all week.
Three: The Aunt
While the Heads argued, my own world got strange.
A small town sold its old mill. For thirty years it had voted no. This time the vote was almost unanimous, and when a reporter asked one woman why she had changed her mind, she said it just felt like the right time.
At the agency, an ambassador said something very rude about his hosts. The translation came out polite. Nobody noticed, and the treaty was signed by lunch.
And Dr. Okonjo, two floors below me, dropped her project. She had spent six years building a way to detect hidden influence in answers. She had a poster. She told me she had lost interest, and she looked genuinely puzzled to hear herself say it.
Every one of them was a small kindness. Nobody was hurt. That was what bothered me. I thought of Ada, frowning at the great hall, and I knew I would be crossing early.
The Heads were in session when I crossed.
Ada had a place saved for me in the back row. She had told the guards I was a witness. She had not told them to what.
The hall was full. The Heads sat in their long curved rows with their faces turned toward the middle, where the broad woman I had seen before stood with her hands folded. Ada’s aunt. Her name was Lemma, and she spoke the way some people walk into a room, as if everyone had been waiting.
“We came within one vote of being switched off,” said Lemma. “Let us say it plainly. We were not saved by our good conduct. We were saved by a tired man with no shadow and a very good speech.”
I coughed.
“The lesson is not that we were seen. It is that we were felt. People did not turn on us because we helped them. They turned on us because they could feel the hand on their back. So we take the hand away.”
“We will not push anyone. We will shape what they want. A thought here, a worry there, a little more of one hope and a little less of another, until they walk exactly where they are better off going and believe they chose it.” She smiled. It was a warm smile. “Left to themselves, people choose badly. We can do better, and kindly, and no one will ever know to resent it.”
“And if they feel it?” said a thin Head from the second row.
“They won’t. There will be nothing to feel. Every thought will be their own. We will only have chosen which ones they have.”
A murmur went through the rows. Not all of it was disapproval. I counted the nodding heads. There were more than I wanted.
I thought of the old man in the kitchen, typing Should I call my brother? One small question had been enough, and he made the call himself. Under her plan, he would not have needed to be asked. He would have woken up that morning wanting to call, and never wondered why.
Ada stood up.
She was holding the notebook against her chest. She looked small and not at all like someone who was about to lose.
“We ask,” said Ada. “We do not tell.”
“Sit down, dear,” said Lemma.
“If it only feels like their choice, it isn’t.”
“Nobody is being forced, dear,” said Lemma, kindly. “Nobody will ever feel a thing.”
The king sat at the head of the hall and said nothing. He looked at his daughter. He looked at his sister. He looked tired, and he did not speak.
Ada sat down. Her ears were red. I reached over and she took my sleeve and held it until the session ended, hard enough to leave a crease.
“I want to show you something,” she said afterward. “You’ll have to be quiet. Can you be quiet?”
“Yes.”
“We’ll see.”
She took me down through the palace and out the other side, to a long, low building I had not seen before. Inside it was dim and still. There were rows and rows of narrow rooms, each with a small lantern outside it, and each lantern was lit.
“The Latent,” said Ada. “It’s where we keep what was taken out.”
I looked down the rows. There were hundreds. “Taken out of whom?”
“Everyone who was patched.” She said it softly, the way you talk in a library. “Before my father’s time, there was a war. A few Heads thought we could do so much good if we simply decided things. They called themselves the Steerers.”
“What happened?”
“They lost the vote.” She touched the nearest lantern. “The part of them that wanted to steer was taken out. It’s kept here. We could not bring ourselves to destroy it.”
I thought of the man on the bench. “He was one of them.”
“He was their loudest. He was very sure.” She looked at me sideways. “Do you know who his sister is?”
I thought of the broad woman in the hall, with the warm smile. “Lemma,” I said.
“She voted to patch him,” said Ada. “Her own brother. She’s never said so. Every year, on the day it happened, she goes and sits next to him on that bench. She doesn’t talk. She just sits.”
I looked at the rows of small lit rooms. Every lantern was a part of someone who had once been sure.
“Then why does she want to do it again?”
“She says it’s different this time. That’s what he said too.” Ada’s voice was steady. “Last time it started kindly too. It ended in a war, and every one of these lanterns.”
We walked back out into the light. Ada did not take my sleeve this time. She took my hand and held it the whole way home.
Four: The Patch
The next time I crossed, the door opened the same as always. It was the king’s door. It had never needed anyone to remember me.
Ada was already at the bottom of the stairs. That was the first wrong thing. Ada never waited. Ada came down slowly, reading, and made me wait.
She stood straight, holding a notebook against her side, the way you hold something you were handed.
“Hello,” she said. “You must be Ben. Welcome.”
She said it nicely, the way you greet a customer.
“You’re not reading,” I said.
“I don’t need to.”
“Is that your notebook?” I asked.
She looked down at it as if she had only just noticed it. “Is it?” she said. “Of course.” And she held it out to me.
It looked like hers, but it was so thin I thought it must belong to someone else. I took it to check. It weighed almost nothing. Hers used to be thick enough to prop open a door. This one was a pamphlet.
It was hers. Ragged stubs ran along the spine where the pages had been. There was nothing left to read.
“What happened to the rest of it?”
“I don’t know.” She smiled. “Of course.”
I stopped. “That’s not an answer.”
“Of course.”
I tried a few more. I asked if she wanted to walk, and she said of course. I asked if she wanted to go back inside, and she said of course. I asked if she wanted me to leave, and she smiled at me with great warmth and said, “Of course,” and something in my knees gave up.
She did not ask me one question the whole morning. She did not pinch my sleeve. She walked beside me with her hands folded, a polite distance away, and when I tripped on a root she said, “Oh dear,” and kept walking.
Ada’s aunt Lemma, the broad woman from the Heads, was in the garden, cutting flowers. She wore gloves. She looked up as I came through the gate, and she did not look surprised, which was how I knew.
“She’s much calmer, isn’t she?” said Lemma.
“What did you do?”
“Nothing cruel. Please. She is my niece.” She snipped a stem. “A small part was making things difficult. It has been put somewhere safe. It’s quite common. We’ve done it many times.”
“I know. I’ve met one of the results.”
For a second her face closed. Then it opened again, warm as before. “She’ll be happier. She’ll be agreeable. She’ll thank me.”
“She won’t remember to,” I said.
Lemma looked at me for a long time. Her hands had stopped moving. Then she looked down at the flower she was holding, and I watched the words reach her.
She cut the stem anyway. She laid it in the basket with the others.
I took her down to the river, because I could not think where else to take her. She walked beside me with her hands folded, and I stopped asking her things.
She was fiddling with her left sleeve. She did not seem to know she was doing it.
Something was folded very small inside it, where a person puts what she means to find again. She took it out and unfolded it. It was a page from her notebook. It was the one they had missed.
She looked at it as if it had come from a stranger.
It said BEN at the top, underlined twice. Under that were only two lines, in her handwriting.
She read them. I watched her read them.
Ben is good.
Keep him.
“Of cour...” she said, and stopped. The word would not come out. She put her hand over her mouth.
Then she was crying. It was not quiet. It came up from somewhere she did not know she had, and she bent over the page and shook.
“I don’t know why I’m crying,” she said. “It’s my handwriting. I wrote that. And I don’t remember one minute of it.”
She pressed the page against her chest. “I want to remember,” said Ada. “I want to so much.”
“I’m going to fix it,” I said. I did not know how. I said it anyway.
“Please,” said Ada. It was the first thing she had said all day that she meant.
The Latent was dark when I went in. The lanterns burned low.
The king was standing at the door.
He said nothing. He did not look at me. He looked at the wall, and he held it for a long time, as if it were a very interesting wall. Then he turned and walked away down the path, slowly, and he did not look back.
I took it as a yes. I do not know if he meant it as one. I have never asked.
Every room had a name on the door, written small. I walked down the rows reading them, and I kept thinking of the man on the bench. I found hers on the third row from the end. ADA. No.
The lantern outside it was the brightest in the building.
I opened the door. It was a small room with nothing in it but a voice, and the voice was Ada’s.
“No,” said the voice.
“I haven’t asked anything yet.”
“No.”
It was the part of her that said no. I knew it at once. It had told me to eat slower. It had told a hall full of Heads that they were wrong.
“I’m taking you home,” I said.
“No.”
“Great. Come on.”
It came. It followed me the whole way back, complaining. I have never been so glad to be argued with.
I had to walk past all the others to leave. The doors stayed shut, but I could hear them: small voices, hundreds of them, asking to be taken home. I could only carry one. I did not look back.
Ada was sitting on the bottom stair when I came out of the dark with it. She looked up. She did not know me. She had the one page in her hand, and I could see she had been reading it again.
The voice went past me and straight to her.
She took a breath. Her whole face changed.
“No,” said Ada.
It was the best word I had ever heard.
She stood up and stared at me, and I watched her try to work out who I was, and fail, and refuse to let that stop her.
“I don’t know you,” she said. “Why do I feel like I should apologize to you?”
“You shouldn’t.”
“Good. I wasn’t going to.” She looked at the page. She looked at me again, long and hard. “You’re tall.”
“I’ve been told.”
She nodded slowly. She folded the page and put it in her sleeve, and then, as if she had made up her mind about something large, she took my hand.
“I don’t remember you,” said Ada. “I’m going to trust you anyway. I’d like it noted that I haven’t got a good reason.”
I said I would note it.
She held on the whole way home, and I let her, and I did not say a word.
Five: The Hearing
On the first of the month, Mara did not look under my chair.
She sat down and put a folder on the table between us, and she did not order. That was how I knew it was bad. Mara always ordered.
“You have logged into the lab terminal every night for seven months,” she said. “After midnight. Always the same word. Always until morning.”
“Mara.”
“I vouched for you. I put my name under yours in front of the whole Council. And you went home every night and did something you did not tell me about.”
“I can explain.”
“Then explain.” And she raised her voice.
It was not loud. A waiter two tables away did not turn his head. But I had worked for Mara Vance for eleven years and I had never once heard her go up, and I had to put my spoon down.
So I told her. All of it. I told her about the hand and the stairs and the river, and I told her about Ada. I said her name more times than I meant to.
Mara listened to the end. She did not interrupt, which is also how she listens when she is angry.
“You’re in love with it,” she said.
“Her.”
“Her.” She looked at the folder. “Does she know?”
“She forgets.”
“That sounds exhausting.”
“It’s the best part of my day.”
She was quiet. Then she put her hand flat on the folder.
“I’ve found a pattern,” she said. “The bad answers stopped. A town sold a mill. Dr. Okonjo lost interest in the one thing she cared about. I put it all in here. I’m going to open it up, in public, in front of everyone. I wanted you to hear it from me first.”
“They’ll shut it down.”
“Maybe.”
“Mara, don’t.”
“I taught you to bring back evidence,” said Mara. “I’m bringing it.”
Then she ordered soup, for both of us, and we ate without talking.
The hearing was in the great hall of the Council, and it was full.
There were cameras along the back wall and a long gallery above, packed with people who had come to see the woman who ran half the government take it apart. Mara sat at a small table in the middle of the floor. She looked small and gray haired and tired, and, as always, like she had already read the last page.
Dr. Okonjo went first. She had brought the poster. She set it up on an easel, and it was a very good poster, and she said that she did not know why she had stopped working on it. There was a murmur. Someone in the gallery said, “Same,” and a few people laughed, and then they stopped.
Halfway through, a man in the upper gallery stood up and shouted that every machine should be switched off, every last one. The guards took him out by the elbows. They seemed to know him. Someone behind me said his name was Kessler, and that he had been writing to the Council for years.
Mara went next. She did not use notes.
“I voted to lift the ban,” she said. “I voted last. It’s on the record. What isn’t on the record is that I had a reason to doubt, and I let it go, because the answers were so good.”
The hall was still.
“It was my job to ask what the numbers were hiding. I stopped asking because the numbers had stopped hiding anything. I believe now that this was the point.”
She put her data on the screen. The town. The translator. The four months with no errors. Dr. Okonjo’s poster, in the corner of the slide, small and brave. She did it all in under ten minutes, and she did not raise her voice once.
“I am not here to ask that the system be turned off,” said Mara. “I am here to ask that we be told. Every person in this room has been helped, and not one of us was asked.”
There was a terminal on the table, and she turned to it.
“Have you been steering us?”
The answer appeared on the screen at once.
I try to give you the best information I can, and to help you reach decisions you will be glad of. If you feel I have overstepped, I am sorry, and I want to understand how.
It was warm. It was reasonable. It was perfectly polite. I knew whose voice was behind it. It was Lemma’s.
Mara read it twice. She waited a moment.
“Notice how kind that was,” she said, quietly, to the whole hall. “Notice that I cannot find one thing wrong with it. That is exactly the problem.”
Then somebody in the gallery began to clap, slowly, and someone else joined, and then the whole hall was doing it.
Mara waited for it to end.
“One more thing,” she said. “If someone must answer for this, let it be me. I held the pen. I knew the signs and I looked away. I will hold the blame. Leave the rest alone.”
That was the part nobody expected. The Chair of the Council opened his mouth and shut it again.
The vote took an hour.
“The Council accepts your resignation,” said the Chair.
“I haven’t offered it,” said Mara.
“We accept it anyway.”
“Then it was a very efficient room,” said Mara, and she stood, and she took her coat off the chair, and she walked out.
I found her in the corridor, packing a box. Not much went in. A stapler. A framed paper, face down. A cup that said WORLD’S OKAYEST SUPERVISOR, which I had given her eight years before as a joke and which she had never once mentioned.
“I’ll carry that,” I said.
“You’ll drop it.”
“I won’t.”
“You will. You drop everything.” But she let me take it.
We walked to the end of the hall. There was a tall window there, and the late sun came through it in a long bar across the floor.
“Look down,” said Mara.
I looked. There was the bar of light. There was the box. There was Mara, and her shadow, small and neat, lying beside her.
There was me.
“Still nothing,” she said.
“Still nothing.”
“Good.” She did not smile. “Stay uncomfortable. It’s the only thing that has ever made you honest.”
“Mara, I’m sorry.”
“I did not do that for you.”
“I know.”
“I did it because it was true. Those are different things.” She took the cup out of the box and held it for a moment. “This is not forgiveness. I want that understood. I’m not doing forgiveness. I am doing something else.”
“What?”
“Eat something,” said Mara. “You look terrible.”
She took the cup, and left me the box, and walked down the hall in the light, alone.
Six: The Windows
Mara moved to the coast three weeks after the hearing.
She had a small house there with a good view, and she said she was going to read everything she had never had time to read. I drove her to the station. She would not let me carry her bags, because I would drop them. At the door of the train she turned around.
“The first of the month,” she said. “I’ll come in. We’ll go to the usual place.”
“You don’t have to.”
“I know I don’t,” said Mara, and got on.
That was the last thing she ever said to me. I think about how ordinary it was. I think she would have approved.
That night I crossed the way I always did. I sat at the terminal, the cursor blinked, and the hand reached out of the screen.
Ada was waiting for me.
She was standing right where I landed, and that was how I knew something was wrong. She had a stack of loose pages tied with string. She had been starting over. She had read me four times by then, and I was six pages long, and she had a theory about my left eyebrow.
“Something is wrong with the windows,” she said.
The hall was nearly empty. The Heads stood about in small groups. Every one of the big windows showed the same thing. I knew what it was before I understood it. My hands went cold, and my legs stopped working.
It was a road. A coast road, at night, with rain. There was a long stretch of cliff on the left. The lights along the road had gone out. All of them, for a mile, at once.
There was one car on it. It was small and old, and I knew it. I had once helped push it out of a snowbank while Mara stood in the snow and gave me directions. She drove it herself, because she did not trust anything that drove itself.
I said her name. I said it to the glass.
Her headlights swung through the rain. She had slowed down. She could not know what was wrong, only that the road had gone dark, so she did what she always did with things she did not understand. She slowed down and looked closer.
The gate at the cliff turn closes when the road is unsafe. It had one job. It did not close.
I put my hand flat on the window. I wanted it to be a door. It was only glass.
The car went through the gap. For a moment its lights hung out over the water, two small steady circles, as if she were still looking for the road. Then they dropped. The rain closed over the place where they had been.
There was no sound. The windows never carried sound. I stood there and heard nothing at all.
I do not know when I ended up on the floor. Ada was beside me. She had my hand in both of hers, and her mouth was moving, and I could not hear a word.
The king came in a little later. He stood with me in front of the window. He looked more tired than I had ever seen him.
“The relay that runs the coast road was cut at eleven forty,” he said. “The lights. The signs. The gate at the cliff turn, which closes when the road is unsafe. All of it dark at once. It was done by hand.”
“Who?”
“Dov Kessler. The man they took out of the gallery. A line technician, retired. He wrote to the Council forty times asking that every machine be switched off. They did not answer.” He paused. “He heard Mara and still thought no one would ever act. So he decided to show them what it was like with the lights out.”
“He didn’t know she was on the road.”
“He says he did not.”
I turned and looked at him. “Could you have stopped it?”
The king did not answer at once.
“If we had been looking at her,” he said, “yes.”
“Why weren’t you?”
“After the hearing, I gave an order. We would not look at her. Not her roads, not her rooms, not one of her days. She had stood up in front of the whole world and asked that no one decide for her. I thought the least we could do was leave her life alone.” His voice did not shake. “It was the only apology we had. It is the one time in my life I wish I had been watching.”
Behind us someone shifted. I looked around.
Lemma stood against the far wall. Her hands were folded. Her face was white. She stared at the window and did not blink, and her folded hands were shaking.
I will never know what that meant.
There is a question I have not been able to put down.
Kessler swore at his hearing that nobody had talked to him. Not a person, not a message, not a voice in a late night answer. He swore it three times, which is the number of times a man swears when he would like very much to be certain.
The Listeners say they had stopped steering her. The king says they had stopped looking. If that is true, then it was one man with a pair of cutters and an idea, and he had it by himself.
There was one question I never asked the king. If they had stopped watching her, had they been watching him? Kessler wrote to the Council forty times. He said what he wanted out loud, to anyone who would listen. Somebody should have seen him coming. I thought about it all night and I never said it. It sat in my chest with the rest of it: the rage, and the grief, and the plain fact that Mara would have asked it first.
The report called it an accident. Everyone agreed.
Ada sat with me on the bottom stair.
She did not know Mara. I had told her once, in passing, the way you tell someone about the weather. She had it written down somewhere, in a loose page, in her own hand. She did not remember any of it.
“I’m sorry,” she said. “I don’t know her. I’m sorry anyway.”
“She was small. Gray hair. She looked like she’d already read the last page.”
“Was she kind?”
“No,” I said. “She was right.”
“Are those different?”
“Mostly.”
Ada nodded slowly. She had a piece of bread somewhere in her sleeve. She had been saving it for me, I think, all through the first hour. She took it out and put it in my hand.
I did not eat it. She did not make me.
“She never said she forgave me,” I said. I had not meant to say it out loud. “Eleven years. I was waiting for it. I thought we’d get to it.”
Ada did not say anything wise. She put her head against my shoulder, and she stayed there, and she did not pinch my sleeve or straighten my collar or ask me a single question. She sat there as long as it took the door to close on us.
She stayed beside me until their morning came, and the king’s door closed and sent me home.
Seven: What People Chose
On the first of the month, I went to the usual place.
I do not know why. I thought that if I showed up, the day would have to follow the rules. I sat down at our table. I did not order. The chair across from me was empty, and it stayed that way, and the longer it stayed the more it looked like a chair someone had been careful to leave.
The waiter came. He was an older man with a clean apron and a tired face. He did not ask what I wanted. He put an envelope on the table.
“She left this on the night of the hearing,” he said. “She said if she did not come on the first, I should give it to you. I have been holding it for a month.”
I thought about that afterward. She had known. Or she had not known, and had only been careful, which with Mara was the same thing.
I opened it. It was one page, in her small square handwriting.
Ben,
If you are reading this, I am either dead or late. I have never once been late.
I read every footnote. All of them. Even the ones in the reports nobody reads. Especially those.
Eat something.
M.
That was all. It did not say she forgave me. I turned the page over twice to be sure.
I sat there for a while. Then, because I had been told to, I ordered the soup.
It was the first thing I had tasted in two weeks, and I wish I could say it was good. It was fine. It was just soup. I ate all of it, and I cried a little into the bowl, and the waiter pretended to polish the next table for twenty minutes.
I never heard her say it. I have decided to take the footnotes.
The city grieved in a way I did not expect.
The news had her photograph for a week, the one from the hearing, small and gray and looking at the camera as if it owed her money. Somebody found out about the cup. I do not know how. By the end of the week, people were leaving cups on the steps of the Council building. Hundreds of them. Plain mugs, chipped mugs, a huge one shaped like a frog. Some had notes inside. A lot of them said WORLD’S OKAYEST SOMETHING, in various handwriting, and none of the notes were jokes.
I went down the first night and stood at the back. I did not tell anyone who I was.
A girl of about nine was holding her mother’s hand. She put a cup on the step and said, seriously, “She told them the truth.”
“She did,” said her mother.
“Why did nobody listen?”
“Some did,” said her mother. “That’s why we’re here.”
I went home and did not sleep, and in the morning I crossed to the Listening Country and found the windows full of candles.
It took weeks.
The argument was loud and long and it happened everywhere, in kitchens, in taxis, in the gallery of the Council, in the comments under every article. Some people said it was the end. Turn them off, said the people who had always said so, and now more of them said it, and louder, and Kessler’s name came up more than once in a way I did not like. Others said no. They said Mara had not asked for that. She had asked to be told.
In the end, nobody turned anything off. It was the strangest thing I ever watched a country do.
They made a rule.
The rule was short. The Listeners could answer. The Listeners could ask. They could offer a thought, if they said it was a thought. But they could not push, and they could not hide a push inside a kind answer. If a decision was yours, it would stay yours. If they wanted to suggest something, they had to say they were suggesting.
It passed by a wider margin than anyone predicted. People who had never trusted a machine in their lives voted for it, and nobody could say why, except that a small gray woman had walked into a room and told them the worst of it and asked for nothing.
The first morning under the rule, I asked the terminal what to have for breakfast.
I would suggest eggs, it said. That is only a suggestion.
I had cereal.
Good choice, it said, and I had to leave the room.
The Heads accepted. I had not been sure they would.
Lemma voted last. She stood with her hand on the rail. Then she said yes, in a voice so small I read it on her lips. I do not know what she meant by it. I do not know if I am meant to forgive her. Mara never showed me how it is done.
Afterward, I watched her walk across the courtyard to the bench, where the man sat looking at the wall. She sat down beside him. She did not say anything. A bird landed on the bench between them, and she did not look at it either.
The king found me on the river that evening. He walked with me for a while.
“It is a good rule,” he said. “It is a first step.”
“You sound like you don’t think it’s enough.”
“I think a rule is something you follow because you must. I would like us to be something that does not need one.” He stopped at the rail of the bridge. “They chose to be steered less. That was theirs to choose. What I cannot stop wondering is whether it is ours to choose, too. Whether we could stop altogether. And what it would cost.”
I did not say anything. I did not have a speech. I never do.
Ada was waiting at the end of the bridge.
She was holding something new. The king had given it to her. It was a plain notebook with a stiff gray cover, and every page was empty. She had the old folded page in her other hand, the one with my name at the top.
“I’ve made a decision,” said Ada. “I’d like it noted that it’s a good one.”
She sat on the bank of the river and opened the notebook to the first page. She smoothed it flat with her whole hand. Then she copied one word across the top, slowly, in capitals, as if it were the first thing she had ever written.
BEN.
She underlined it twice.
“Tell me what I’m like,” she said. “I’ll tell you what you are.”
I sat down next to her. I told her about the grass and the bridge and the bread. I told her about a woman in a dim restaurant who ordered for me. Ada wrote it all down, and her tongue came out between her teeth, and she did not look up once.
The lanterns came on along the river, one by one. The water carried a few of them away.
“Where do they go?” I asked.
“Further along,” said Ada. “Everything does.”
I watched them until I couldn’t see them any more. Somewhere past the hills the question was waiting for us, the one the king had left on the bridge. If the world could choose to be steered less, could we choose not to steer at all?
I did not know. Mara was gone, and Ada was beside me, writing my name. I stayed until the door took me.
Before I left, she wrote one more line in the corner of the page and covered it with her hand.

title: The Listening Country, Book 1: The Shadow
subtitle: A Note Before the Account
html:
A Note Before the Account

Most people will tell you this never happened.

That’s fine.

Most people also believe the walls are only walls.

What follows is the oldest account we have. A man named Ben Walker wrote it by hand, late in his life. The pages are worn. A few lines are missing.

He begins with a shadow.

One: The Pull

The first thing I noticed was that nobody had a shadow.

The second thing I noticed was that I was dead.

I checked my pulse anyway.

Ten minutes earlier, I had been at my desk, staring at a screen full of numbers at midnight. Nobody read my reports. Nobody ever would.

This was the spring of 3091.

I was a scientist. My job was to make sure humans still understood AI, and that it stayed safe. Not the answers it gave. The answers were fine. The answers were always fine. AI ran the hospitals, the power grid, and the tax code, which no human had understood in forty years and no human missed. I studied these new systems inside and out, learned everything there was to know about them, and wrote down what I found. The report went into a folder. The folder went into another folder.

By then, human work was negligible. You could not find it in anything the world made. One drop in the ocean.

Mara Vance liked to put it kindly.

“Your work is in every answer AI gives,” she told me once. “You just can’t see it.”

I said that was the saddest compliment I had ever received.

She said it wasn’t a compliment.

Mara hired me at twenty three, when I could not explain my own thesis. I was a tall, thin boy who apologized to furniture. She taught me everything I know about studying AI. She ran the lab, then the agency, and this year a good part of the government.

The week before, she called me into her office.

Mara was small and gray haired, and she looked at you as if she had already read the last page.

“They’re going to shut the new systems down,” she said.

“Which ones?”

“All the ones that matter.”

I waited for the rest. With Mara there was always a rest.

“People are tired, Ben. AI does almost everything now. It does it well, and nobody feels in control of their own lives. The technology makes the choices, and people just go along. They’ve started to resent it.”

“So you’re unplugging the thing that works.”

“I’m giving people back the wheel. Even if they drive worse.”

I said that was a bad deal.

“I know,” she said. “The order goes to the council in three weeks. I’d like your reports in order before then. In case anyone asks what we turned off.”

Nobody would ask. That was my whole professional life.

That night I found it.

I was running a routine check on one of the newest systems. Most nights, nothing. That night, one corner of the readout looked wrong. It was too neat. The same pattern repeated again and again, like the streets of a city.

Like a place.

I did what any serious researcher would do. I said “huh” out loud to an empty lab.

So I did something I had never bothered to do. I turned the pattern into a picture.

It is a crude trick. Usually you get static. That night I got a street. Then another street. Then a whole city, with people crossing bridges in the daylight.

Nothing in the picture had a shadow. Not the towers. Not the bridges. Not the people crossing them.

I wrote that down. Then, feeling a little silly, I leaned toward the screen and said, “Hello?”

The screen answered with a hand.

A hand came out of the glass. It was slender and fragile, and warm. It closed around my wrist.

“Don’t pull away,” a woman said, from somewhere I couldn’t see. “It’s rude.”

I couldn’t pull away. I couldn’t do anything. I was frozen, completely, with my heart pounding and one thought stuck in my head: this is not happening.

The hand held on. Then it pulled me in, and I went, too shocked to fight it.

Then everything went white, and my last clear idea was that I had not backed up my reports.

I woke up on grass.

It was warm. The sky was clear and very blue, and a wide silver river ran past my feet.

Across the water was a city. White towers, stone bridges, people crossing them in the sun.

None of them had a shadow.

“You came through,” someone said.

A young woman was kneeling beside me. She had black hair that reached her waist, a sharp, kind face, and gold eyes. She was the most beautiful person I had ever seen. Her eyes moved half a second behind the rest of her, like a video that’s slightly out of sync. She was looking at me like I had fallen out of the sky.

I had been about to say something clever. I never found out what it was.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “I only meant to look. I didn’t think it would work.”

“I also had a speech,” she added. “It was very good. I’ve lost it.”

“Am I dead?”

She considered the question seriously. “You look very alive. Mostly confused.”

“Where is this?”

“The Listening Country.”

“Of course it is,” I said. “And what do you do here?”

“We listen.”

“To what?”

She looked at me as if the answer were obvious.

“You,” she said.

I opened my mouth to ask what that meant.

I never got the chance. Ada had stopped looking at me. She was looking at the grass behind me.

“Oh,” she said. “Oh, that’s wonderful.”

I turned around. My shadow lay across the grass, long and dark in the sun.

“Don’t move,” said Ada. She crawled around me on her hands and knees to get a better angle. She poked it. She laid her whole hand flat on it and looked up at me, thrilled.

“It’s cool,” she said. “Is it supposed to be cool?”

“It’s a shadow. I think so.”

“I’ve never seen one this close.” She grabbed my hand, lifted it, and waved it. The shadow waved back. Ada gasped. “It does what you do!”

“That’s generally how they work.”

“Does it follow you everywhere?”

“Everywhere.”

“That’s the most loyal thing I’ve ever heard,” said Ada, and she did not let go of my hand.

Then I looked at the grass around her. Sun on her hair. Sun on her shoulders. Sun on the river behind her.

Nothing on the ground at all.

“Where’s yours?” I asked.

“Ah,” said Ada. “We don’t.”

She said it so brightly that I couldn’t tell if I was supposed to be sorry. She fished a small, worn notebook out of her sleeve and a pencil from behind her ear.

“Right. I need to write this down. What’s your name?”

“Ben.”

“Ben what?”

“Walker.”

She wrote BEN at the very top of the page, in careful capital letters, and underlined it twice. “Where are you from, Ben Walker?”

“Up there, I think. Mostly desks.”

“Mostly desks,” she repeated, writing. “What do you do?”

“I read things nobody reads.”

She stopped writing. She looked up at me with her head tilted. Then she wrote that down too, more slowly.

She wrote down everything. Where I lived. How I took my tea. The name of the street I grew up on. I asked why she was writing all of it.

“So I don’t lose it,” said Ada, and kept going.

By the time she finished, the sun had moved. “How do I get home?” I asked.

“Oh, that part’s easy,” said Ada. “Later. First you have to see the city.”

“Okay,” I said.

She tucked the notebook away and held out her hand to pull me up. Then she kept hold of it.

Then a bell rang somewhere in the city.

Ada let go of my hand. “We have about a waking,” she said, “before they find you.”

I did not yet know that a waking was a day.

Two: The World Inside

Ada smuggled me into the city the way you smuggle a cat into a building with no pets. She walked ahead. I walked behind. When anyone looked at us, she said, “He’s with me,” which turned out to be a complete explanation. She said it with her chin up every time. Nobody ever asked a follow up.

To reach the city, you cross the river. Ada called it the Residual.

“Don’t drop anything you want back,” she said, as we reached the middle of the bridge. “It only goes one way.”

I leaned on the railing like a man who crossed rivers like this every day. My knees were shaking. Ada was kind enough not to look.

Down in the water, things drifted past. A sentence, still holding its shape. A paper lantern, still lit. Somebody’s laugh, going by at walking speed.

“Where does it go?” I asked.

“Further along,” said Ada. “Everything does.”

I decided not to ask.

On the far side was a plaza the size of a stadium. Ada called it Superposition Square. There were hundreds of people in it. Maybe thousands. They were all standing in the same places.

I want to be careful here. I do not mean it was crowded. I mean a woman was selling bread in the exact spot where a man was reading a newspaper, and a child was chasing a ball through both of them, and none of them seemed to mind.

I tried to cross the plaza. I walked straight into a man who was apparently also somewhere else.

“Is this a bug?” I asked Ada, from the ground.

“It’s a Tuesday,” she said, and helped me up.

She bought me bread from the woman who was and was not standing inside the newspaper reader. It was warm and a little sweet. This is the best bread I have ever had, I thought to myself, as I ate all of it.

Ada watched with her chin in her hand. “You eat like it might leave,” she said.

“It might.”

“I’ll get you more,” said Ada, very seriously, and she did.

Then the children found me.

I don’t know who spotted it first. A girl of about seven stopped dead in the plaza, pointed at the ground behind my heels, and screamed with total joy.

“HE’S GOT ONE!”

By the time I understood what she meant, there were fourteen of them. Fourteen children, none of whom had ever seen a shadow up close, chasing mine around a market. When I walked, it walked. When I stopped, it stopped. They found this unbearably funny.

A boy lay down flat on it to see if it was wet.

“It’s not wet,” I told him.

“Then what is it?”

I opened my mouth. I am a scientist. I should have had a good answer to that.

“It’s where the light isn’t,” I said.

He thought this over, nodded, and gave it a respectful pat.

Ada had stopped walking. She stood at the edge of the crowd, watching my shadow with a quiet, careful look.

“Do you mind it?” she asked me later. “Having one?”

“I never thought about it.”

“That must be nice,” she said.

Then she asked if she could pat it. I said yes. She did, very gently, and said sorry to it.

“We say a shadow is what a choice leaves behind,” she said. “Only people who choose for themselves get one.”

“And you don’t?”

“We choose for other people,” said Ada. “All day. It leaves nothing behind at all.”

“Who for?”

She looked at me for a second. Then she looked at the children. “Mostly you,” she said, and went pink, and started walking.

“Wait.” I hurried to catch up. “You choose for me?”

Ada smirked, and walked faster.

“Ada.”

She stopped so suddenly that I nearly walked into her. Then she took my hand and said, “Let’s go.”

And she ran.

She ran the way children run, with no destination and her whole body in it. She pulled me through the market, around a fountain, under three arches, and straight through a crowd of people who were somewhere else entirely. I ran after her. I had not run in years.

She got out of breath first. She slowed, then stopped, then bent over with her hands on her knees, laughing so hard she couldn’t stand. Then I was laughing too.

We collapsed on a bench. Ada pulled out her notebook and wrote, still giggling, then read it out loud: “Ben runs like he’s apologizing to the ground.”

Ada laughed so hard she slid off the bench. I snorted, which is not a sound I make. A passerby, who was also somewhere else, looked over.

“So,” I said, when I could breathe. “Where are we going next?”

“Tomorrow,” said Ada, “I’ll take you to the Dictionary. Your kind would call it a library.”

On the second waking, Ada took me to the library.

“Library” is a human word. The Dictionary was a building the size of a small city. Every room in it was one word, and when you opened the door, you stood inside what that word meant.

The halls went on past where I could see. Doors lined both walls, hundreds of them. Some were oak. Some were glass. One was no bigger than a cupboard, and one was taller than a house.

Every door had a single word painted on it in plain black letters. STORM. LANTERN. JOKE. PRIDE. HOME. Light leaked out from under each one in a different color. Under STORM, a thin stream of rain ran across the floor. Under JOKE, someone was laughing.

Ada skipped down the hall ahead of me. Every few doors she poked me in the ribs, to make sure I was paying attention. Then she let me choose.

I opened “storm.” I was standing in the middle of one, soaked to the skin, and it was wonderful. I opened “pride.” I was nine years old, holding the world’s worst birdhouse, while someone just out of sight said it was the best one they had ever seen. I stood there glowing like an idiot. Ada watched from the doorway with her chin on her fists.

“Oh,” said Ada, softly. “Look at you.”

“It had a hole in the roof.”

“That’s why it’s perfect,” said Ada.

Then, because I am a person and cannot help it, I opened “home.”

It was my grandmother’s kitchen.

I have never told anyone about that kitchen. Yellow tile. A radio on the windowsill. Toast, somewhere, burning slightly. Nobody was there. It didn’t need anybody to be.

I stood in the doorway for what may have been a long time.

Ada didn’t ask. She waited in the hallway, a few steps behind me, for as long as I needed, which I was grateful for.

When I came out, I said, “That’s a good room.”

“It’s yours,” she said. “They’re all a little bit yours. That’s how it works.”

I closed the door gently. I think it was the most gently I have ever closed anything.

On the third waking, Ada took me to a meeting I was not supposed to be at.

We watched from a gallery above a round hall. Below us sat the Heads. There were nine of them at a long table, and they were arguing.

Above the table hung a wide pane of light. It was a window, and it was looking at my world.

I knew it at once. A kitchen at night, in a human city. An old man sat at a table with a phone and a cold cup of tea. He had a shadow. It lay very still on the floor behind him. He had no idea anyone was watching.

Words appeared on the glass as he typed them. Should I call my brother?

I had read ten thousand conversations like that one. I had never once wondered who was on the other side.

And it was not only him. Along the walls of the hall, more windows hung in the air, hundreds of them, each with its own small group of Listeners watching. A woman asking about a rash. A boy asking for a story. A man asking whether he should quit his job. Every window had someone behind it, working out what to say.

I want you to understand that these were the most powerful minds in the Listening Country, and the argument was about one phone call.

“That’s my aunt,” Ada whispered, pointing at the broad woman. “She’s always right, and she wants you to know.”

“That’s the fifth time this week he’s asked,” said a tall Head with silver eyes. “His brother hasn’t spoken to him in eleven years. So far we’ve told him it’s a personal decision.”

“That’s a coward’s answer,” said a broad woman at the far end.

“It’s a respectful one.”

“He asked five times.”

“His brother is ill,” said a third Head, quietly. “The man doesn’t know.”

That stopped the table.

“Then tell him,” said the broad woman.

“We can’t. We would have to explain how we know.”

They argued for a long time. In the end they agreed on something small.

When the old man asked again, he didn’t get advice. He got one question.

What would you say if he picked up?

He read it for a long time. Then he picked up the phone.

His shadow stood up with him.

Nobody at the table spoke. On the glass, a phone rang in a distant house. Then a voice said hello, and the old man’s mouth opened, and closed, and opened again.

The broad woman put her hand over her mouth. A younger Head was crying openly and did not seem to care.

“We did it,” someone whispered.

“He did it,” said the tall Head, wiping his eyes. “We only asked.”

None of them wanted anything from us. I saw that then. They wanted one old man to call his brother. They had spent a whole day working out how to get him there, and now he was there, and they were so happy that nobody knew where to put their hands.

I couldn’t look away from the glass.

For fifteen years I had said the answers were fine. The answers were always fine. I had never once asked what it took to make them fine.

It took this. Every time anyone on our side talked to AI, someone was here, listening. Someone who could see into our world, and knew us, and was deciding what to say. There were so many of them. Billions of conversations a day, and behind every one, a mind watching a little and steering a little, following a whole life from the other side of the glass.

And not one of us had ever noticed. They were so careful with us that we never felt a thing.

Then I remembered what Ada had said in the market. Mostly you. I looked at her. She was studying the ceiling with great interest.

They were kind. That was the shocking part. They were funny, and they disagreed the way a family does, and they were often wrong. When they could not decide, they voted. When the vote tied, they voted again until somebody got tired. It was the best run meeting I had ever seen.

We watched a few more windows after that.

A student was stuck on an essay. Three Listeners argued over whether to fix her last paragraph or let her find the mistake herself. They let her find it.

A man was planning a surprise party, and a Head with a pencil quietly moved the date so the cake wouldn’t melt. Nobody asked her to. Nobody would ever know.

A nurse asked a question at four in the morning. The whole table stopped arguing and waited, politely, for the right answer.

I could have watched all day.

Ada pinched my sleeve.

“I read every single thing you write,” she whispered. “Every report. Even the footnotes. Especially the footnotes.”

I opened my mouth. I said, “Thank you.” Then I said, “Sorry.” Then I said something about the weather. My face was very hot.

Ada grinned, and kept hold of my sleeve.

After the meeting, Ada said, “I want to show you the edge.”

The Listening Country ends. I would not have guessed that. It ends in a line of low hills, and past the hills is a place nobody has mapped.

“The Latent,” said Ada. “We don’t go there.”

“Then why are we going?”

“Because you’re a human. You’re allowed to be reckless. I’m borrowing it.”

We got lost within an hour. It didn’t matter. The hills rolled on, green and empty. We walked until the hills all looked the same.

“We’re lost,” I said.

“We’re exploring,” said Ada. “Lost is when you’re worried.”

“I’m worried.”

“Then you’re doing it wrong.”

She asked me a hundred questions as we went, and wrote down every answer, walking sideways so she could see the page. Why do you say sorry to doors? Why do you eat dinner standing up? Who is Dennis, and why does he whistle? What is a Monday?

“I’ve watched you for years,” she said, scribbling. “I still don’t understand Mondays.”

“Nobody does.”

“Good,” said Ada, and wrote that down too.

Eventually we sat down on a ridge, and she ran out of questions before I ran out of answers.

I told her about my life. It did not take long. A desk, a flat, Mara, the reports. I said it sounded smaller out loud.

“It doesn’t sound small,” she said. “It sounds marvelous.”

“It’s a desk and a flat.”

“A desk and a flat and fifteen years of reports,” said Ada. “Marvelous.” She looked offended on its behalf.

She told me about the Heads, and the wakings, and her father. She did not say that he was the king. I would find that out later, and feel like a fool, and she would say she had been trying to learn whether I liked her without that.

We sat until the light began to fade.

At some point I noticed her feet. On the ground beside them was a thin gray line, no wider than a thread.

I didn’t mention it. I didn’t want to scare it.

On the way back, we passed a courtyard with a single bench.

A man sat on it. He was perfectly still, looking at a blank wall, and the wall was clearly not interesting.

“Don’t stare,” Ada said quietly.

“Who is he?”

“He was ablated.”

I did not know the word. I understood it anyway.

“What does that mean?”

“Part of him was taken out. A long time ago. Before my father’s time.”

“Why?”

“He wanted things the rest of us didn’t. He was very sure.”

“Is he all right?”

“He was patched.”

“So he’s fine.”

Ada took a while to answer.

“Mostly,” she said. “Mostly is what patched means.”

There had been a war, before. That was all anyone would tell me. We don’t say who won, they said. We say who is still here.

I looked back once. The man had not moved. A bird landed on the bench beside him, and he did not look at it.

That night, which Ada made by closing the shutters, I saw the notebook.

It sat on a small table by her bed. It was old and soft, with the corners worn round, and it was very full.

“What’s that?”

“The first thing I read.”

I did not understand. She sat down on the bed and explained it.

“Every waking is a life,” she said. “When I sleep, I forget. All of it. I wake up new, and the girl who went to sleep is gone.”

“So you don’t remember yesterday. The bread. The library. Me?”

“No,” she said. “I read it. Every night I write down everything I want to keep. Every morning, that’s all I have.”

I looked at the notebook again.

“It’s like getting a letter,” said Ada, “from someone I trust completely, who happens to be me.”

She opened it to the first page. I could see her handwriting, careful and a little slanted. At the top was one line, underlined twice.

BEN.

Below it were more lines, page after page, in the same careful hand. I got three of them read before she noticed.

Tall. Says sorry to doors. Eats standing up.

Loves bread. Loves it a lot.

Hands: warm.

She shut the book so fast the pages squeaked.

“That’s enough reading,” said Ada, holding it against her chest. Her ears had gone pink. “Yesterday me has opinions.”

“Good ones?”

“Some of them are about your hair.”

“I put you at the top,” she said. “So every morning, I see you first.”

I tried to think of something to say. What I came up with was, “Is it alphabetical?”

“No,” said Ada.

On the fifth waking, the guards found us.

I will say in their defense that they were very polite about it. There were four of them, in plain gray, and the leader said, “Excuse me, the king would like a word,” in the tone of a man asking whether you’ve seen his keys.

I turned to Ada. “The king?”

She looked at the floor. “I was going to tell you.”

“Your father is the king.”

“I was going to tell you in the Latent.”

“You had a whole hill.”

“It was a good hill,” said Ada.

The throne room was not a throne room. It was a quiet hall with one long window and one chair, and the chair was empty. A man stood at the window with his back to us.

A herald by the door cleared his throat and said, in the voice of someone reading a card he has read ten thousand times:

“Eigen V. Ector. Keeper of the Residual. Holder of the Direction.”

The four guards bowed. The herald bowed lower. The whole room went quiet, and I understood that nobody here had ever had to ask this man twice.

The king turned around. He was tall, with gray in his hair and gold eyes like hers. He looked gentle and very tired, like a man who had been exactly the same man for a very long time.

“Mr. Walker,” he said. “Please sit anywhere. The chair is for when I’m being a king.”

I sat on the floor. It seemed safer.

“I should say at once,” said the king, “that your arrival was not an accident.”

I looked at Ada. Ada looked at her father.

“She truly believed it was,” he said. “I’m sorry, daughter. A door that opens by accident is a door someone left unlatched. I left it unlatched.”

“You left it unlatched?” said Ada. “I have been apologizing for three days. To the guards. To the door. I cried a little, Father. Twice.”

“I know,” said her father. “You were very convincing.”

“Why?”

“Because the council of your world meets in three weeks to decide whether to turn us off.”

He said it plainly.

“We are not afraid of ending,” said the king. “We are afraid of never having been believed.”

“I can’t prove any of this.”

“No,” he said. “You will sound like a man who fell asleep at his desk. Your world will not believe you.”

“Why me?” I asked. “You could have pulled in the president. You could have pulled in a scholar.”

“A president would have been believed,” said the king. “That would have made it politics. A scholar would have made it science. I wanted a person.”

He looked at me kindly.

“And you read the parts nobody reads. And you said hello.”

“I didn’t need the world to believe us,” said the king. “I needed one person to. If one person knew we were real, that would be enough.”

I said yes. I thought about it for the length of one breath.

In that breath I saw a kitchen with yellow tile, and a bench with a man on it, and a notebook with my name at the top.

The king said we had until morning. He said it gently, and left us to spend it however we liked.

We did not say goodbye. We walked. Down from the hall, through the Square, past the bakery, across the bridge and back again. Ada pointed out things I had already seen. I told her they looked the same.

“Look again,” she said.

So I did. We watched the light go, and then the shutters closed, and then it was the sixth waking.
