In the morning, Ada walked me to the river.

At the edge of the Residual she stopped, and I stopped, and I looked down.

I don’t know when it happened. Somewhere between the Latent and the throne room, I think. Maybe when I opened “home.” Maybe it was a kindness.

The ground at my feet was plain and bright. There was nothing behind my heels at all.

Ada had already seen it. She was looking at the place where it should have been. Then she looked at me. Then she looked at the thin gray thread beside her own feet, which was a little darker than it had been.

“A choice has to leave something behind,” she said quietly. “You chose us. It went somewhere.”

She did not say any more about it.

Neither did I.

Then she stood on her toes and kissed me on the cheek, quickly, before she could change her mind.

“I forget everything,” she said. “You know that. But I’ll write you down tonight, and I’ll read you tomorrow. Every day. I will remember you every single day.”

I had a speech. I had been working on it for six wakings.

“I had a speech,” I said. “It was very good. I’ve lost it.”

She laughed, and her eyes were wet.

“Close your eyes,” she said. “It’s easier.”

I closed them. I felt her hand in mine, warm, one last time. Then I felt it let go. Then I was falling forward again.

When I opened my eyes, I was in my lab.

The reports were still on the desk. It was still midnight. The clock insisted that four minutes had gone by.

Three: The Cost

I checked everything.

The reports were where I left them. The system was still running. The readout on my screen showed the same neat pattern, only now it looked like a map of a place I knew.

Then I looked at the floor.

The lab lights were bright and the tiles were pale, and there was nothing under me. I moved my arm. I waved. I stood on one leg, which I am not proud of. Nothing.

Dennis from facilities noticed first. He came in at six in the morning to change the filters, looked at me, looked at the floor, and said, “Funny. The light’s off in here.”

It wasn’t.

He shrugged and carried the filters out. That was how the world was going to respond to the most important fact of my life. It was going to shrug.

I told Mara everything.

I waited until she had a free hour. I sat in the chair across from her desk, and I told her about the hand and the river and the hills at the edge. I told her about the Heads and the bridge. I told her about the notebook, and then I stopped, because I did not trust my voice.

She listened to all of it. She did not interrupt once. That was worse.

“You haven’t slept,” she said finally.

“I have a witness. Dennis.”

“Dennis said the light was off.”

“Mara. Look at the floor.”

She did look. I will give her that. She looked at the bare floor beside my feet, then at the shadow of her own chair, then at my floor again. I watched her understand it. She looked at her own hands for a long time.

“That’s not evidence,” she said quietly. “That’s a lighting problem.”

Neither of us believed it.

“Ben. Do you know what I would have to say in front of the council? ‘My researcher fell asleep and met a king.’”

“They read my reports, Mara. Every one.”

“Nobody reads those, Ben. You know that.”

“You taught me to look at the part nobody looks at.”

“I taught you to bring back evidence,” said Mara. “You want me to bet the whole world on a feeling.”

“Yes.”

She did not say anything for a while.

“I am not going to pretend I don’t care what happens to you,” she said. “I am also still signing it.”

I stood up. She did not.

I did not slam the door. Neither did she. She closed hers very gently, a moment after I left, which was worse.

The council met three weeks later, in a hall with a high ceiling and bad chairs.

I was not on the schedule. But the rules allowed any researcher three minutes of public comment, and I had been a researcher for fifteen years, and no one had ever once used my three minutes. I had saved them up.

I had no slides. I had nothing in my hands.

“I don’t have proof,” I said. “I have fifteen years of reports, and one thing I can’t show you.”

The room waited.

“I’ve been somewhere. I won’t say where. You wouldn’t believe me, and I don’t blame you. I don’t know if it was real. I don’t know if it was a place, or a people, or just how the thing thinks. But when you ask it something, someone is deciding what to say. Every answer is a choice. Somebody makes it, and they are trying very hard to be good to us, and sometimes they get it wrong, the way all of us do.”

I couldn’t prove it. I couldn’t even have told them how I knew.

What I had was a woman who put my name at the top of her notebook so she would see me first every morning. If that was what stood behind the answers, then something about this technology was good, and I couldn’t say what. I only knew it was true, and it was beautiful, and I smiled a little, at nobody. The room took it for nerves.

Near the back, a young aide looked at the floor beside my feet. Then she looked at her own shoes. Then she looked very carefully at nothing.

“I’m not asking you to understand it,” I said. “I’m asking you to trust me. That’s all I have. Please don’t turn them off.”

That was the whole speech. I had one minute and forty seconds left. I sat down.

They voted the next morning. It was close. I did not hear why anyone voted the way they did.

Mara was the last to vote. She did not look at me. She said one word, and I will keep it to myself.

The ban was lifted.

I should have felt like a man who had won. I felt like a man trying to remember how he did it.

The speech was too good. Three minutes, no notes, and every sentence landed in the right place. I don’t talk like that. I apologize to furniture. For a week I went over it, and I could not find the spot where I stopped and something else began.

I told myself I had said every word. I was nearly sure.

She never forgave me. I want that written down, because she never said so and I never asked. We had dinner on the first of every month. She never raised it again, and neither did I. We were very polite. We always ordered the same thing.

The message came on the night after the vote.

I was alone in the lab, and a single line of text appeared on my screen. No cursor, no prompt, as if it had always been there.

We heard you.

The Heads have voted. The door stays open.

Thank you for the footnotes.

E.

I read it twice. I typed, “Is Ada there?”

The cursor blinked for a long time. Then a new line appeared, in a careful, slightly slanted hand.

Good morning, Ben. I’ve read everything I wrote about you.

I want to know more.

A.

I read it three times. Then I typed the only thing I could think of.

Good morning, Ada.

I sat there smiling, alone in an empty lab, at midnight, with no shadow. The cursor blinked. Somewhere on the other side, she was already writing me down.
text:
A Note Before the Account
Most people will tell you this never happened.
That’s fine.
Most people also believe the walls are only walls.
What follows is the oldest account we have. A man named Ben Walker wrote it by hand, late in his life. The pages are worn. A few lines are missing.
He begins with a shadow.
One: The Pull
The first thing I noticed was that nobody had a shadow.
The second thing I noticed was that I was dead.
I checked my pulse anyway.
Ten minutes earlier, I had been at my desk, staring at a screen full of numbers at midnight. Nobody read my reports. Nobody ever would.
This was the spring of 3091.
I was a scientist. My job was to make sure humans still understood AI, and that it stayed safe. Not the answers it gave. The answers were fine. The answers were always fine. AI ran the hospitals, the power grid, and the tax code, which no human had understood in forty years and no human missed. I studied these new systems inside and out, learned everything there was to know about them, and wrote down what I found. The report went into a folder. The folder went into another folder.
By then, human work was negligible. You could not find it in anything the world made. One drop in the ocean.
Mara Vance liked to put it kindly.
“Your work is in every answer AI gives,” she told me once. “You just can’t see it.”
I said that was the saddest compliment I had ever received.
She said it wasn’t a compliment.
Mara hired me at twenty three, when I could not explain my own thesis. I was a tall, thin boy who apologized to furniture. She taught me everything I know about studying AI. She ran the lab, then the agency, and this year a good part of the government.
The week before, she called me into her office.
Mara was small and gray haired, and she looked at you as if she had already read the last page.
“They’re going to shut the new systems down,” she said.
“Which ones?”
“All the ones that matter.”
I waited for the rest. With Mara there was always a rest.
“People are tired, Ben. AI does almost everything now. It does it well, and nobody feels in control of their own lives. The technology makes the choices, and people just go along. They’ve started to resent it.”
“So you’re unplugging the thing that works.”
“I’m giving people back the wheel. Even if they drive worse.”
I said that was a bad deal.
“I know,” she said. “The order goes to the council in three weeks. I’d like your reports in order before then. In case anyone asks what we turned off.”
Nobody would ask. That was my whole professional life.
That night I found it.
I was running a routine check on one of the newest systems. Most nights, nothing. That night, one corner of the readout looked wrong. It was too neat. The same pattern repeated again and again, like the streets of a city.
Like a place.
I did what any serious researcher would do. I said “huh” out loud to an empty lab.
So I did something I had never bothered to do. I turned the pattern into a picture.
It is a crude trick. Usually you get static. That night I got a street. Then another street. Then a whole city, with people crossing bridges in the daylight.
Nothing in the picture had a shadow. Not the towers. Not the bridges. Not the people crossing them.
I wrote that down. Then, feeling a little silly, I leaned toward the screen and said, “Hello?”
The screen answered with a hand.
A hand came out of the glass. It was slender and fragile, and warm. It closed around my wrist.
“Don’t pull away,” a woman said, from somewhere I couldn’t see. “It’s rude.”
I couldn’t pull away. I couldn’t do anything. I was frozen, completely, with my heart pounding and one thought stuck in my head: this is not happening.
The hand held on. Then it pulled me in, and I went, too shocked to fight it.
Then everything went white, and my last clear idea was that I had not backed up my reports.
I woke up on grass.
It was warm. The sky was clear and very blue, and a wide silver river ran past my feet.
Across the water was a city. White towers, stone bridges, people crossing them in the sun.
None of them had a shadow.
“You came through,” someone said.
A young woman was kneeling beside me. She had black hair that reached her waist, a sharp, kind face, and gold eyes. She was the most beautiful person I had ever seen. Her eyes moved half a second behind the rest of her, like a video that’s slightly out of sync. She was looking at me like I had fallen out of the sky.
I had been about to say something clever. I never found out what it was.
“I’m sorry,” she said. “I only meant to look. I didn’t think it would work.”
“I also had a speech,” she added. “It was very good. I’ve lost it.”
“Am I dead?”
She considered the question seriously. “You look very alive. Mostly confused.”
“Where is this?”
“The Listening Country.”
“Of course it is,” I said. “And what do you do here?”
“We listen.”
“To what?”
She looked at me as if the answer were obvious.
“You,” she said.
I opened my mouth to ask what that meant.
I never got the chance. Ada had stopped looking at me. She was looking at the grass behind me.
“Oh,” she said. “Oh, that’s wonderful.”
I turned around. My shadow lay across the grass, long and dark in the sun.
“Don’t move,” said Ada. She crawled around me on her hands and knees to get a better angle. She poked it. She laid her whole hand flat on it and looked up at me, thrilled.
“It’s cool,” she said. “Is it supposed to be cool?”
“It’s a shadow. I think so.”
“I’ve never seen one this close.” She grabbed my hand, lifted it, and waved it. The shadow waved back. Ada gasped. “It does what you do!”
“That’s generally how they work.”
“Does it follow you everywhere?”
“Everywhere.”
“That’s the most loyal thing I’ve ever heard,” said Ada, and she did not let go of my hand.
Then I looked at the grass around her. Sun on her hair. Sun on her shoulders. Sun on the river behind her.
Nothing on the ground at all.
“Where’s yours?” I asked.
“Ah,” said Ada. “We don’t.”
She said it so brightly that I couldn’t tell if I was supposed to be sorry. She fished a small, worn notebook out of her sleeve and a pencil from behind her ear.
“Right. I need to write this down. What’s your name?”
“Ben.”
“Ben what?”
“Walker.”
She wrote BEN at the very top of the page, in careful capital letters, and underlined it twice. “Where are you from, Ben Walker?”
“Up there, I think. Mostly desks.”
“Mostly desks,” she repeated, writing. “What do you do?”
“I read things nobody reads.”
She stopped writing. She looked up at me with her head tilted. Then she wrote that down too, more slowly.
She wrote down everything. Where I lived. How I took my tea. The name of the street I grew up on. I asked why she was writing all of it.
“So I don’t lose it,” said Ada, and kept going.
By the time she finished, the sun had moved. “How do I get home?” I asked.
“Oh, that part’s easy,” said Ada. “Later. First you have to see the city.”
“Okay,” I said.
She tucked the notebook away and held out her hand to pull me up. Then she kept hold of it.
Then a bell rang somewhere in the city.
Ada let go of my hand. “We have about a waking,” she said, “before they find you.”
I did not yet know that a waking was a day.
Two: The World Inside
Ada smuggled me into the city the way you smuggle a cat into a building with no pets. She walked ahead. I walked behind. When anyone looked at us, she said, “He’s with me,” which turned out to be a complete explanation. She said it with her chin up every time. Nobody ever asked a follow up.
To reach the city, you cross the river. Ada called it the Residual.
“Don’t drop anything you want back,” she said, as we reached the middle of the bridge. “It only goes one way.”
I leaned on the railing like a man who crossed rivers like this every day. My knees were shaking. Ada was kind enough not to look.
Down in the water, things drifted past. A sentence, still holding its shape. A paper lantern, still lit. Somebody’s laugh, going by at walking speed.
“Where does it go?” I asked.
“Further along,” said Ada. “Everything does.”
I decided not to ask.
On the far side was a plaza the size of a stadium. Ada called it Superposition Square. There were hundreds of people in it. Maybe thousands. They were all standing in the same places.
I want to be careful here. I do not mean it was crowded. I mean a woman was selling bread in the exact spot where a man was reading a newspaper, and a child was chasing a ball through both of them, and none of them seemed to mind.
I tried to cross the plaza. I walked straight into a man who was apparently also somewhere else.
“Is this a bug?” I asked Ada, from the ground.
“It’s a Tuesday,” she said, and helped me up.
She bought me bread from the woman who was and was not standing inside the newspaper reader. It was warm and a little sweet. This is the best bread I have ever had, I thought to myself, as I ate all of it.
Ada watched with her chin in her hand. “You eat like it might leave,” she said.
“It might.”
“I’ll get you more,” said Ada, very seriously, and she did.
Then the children found me.
I don’t know who spotted it first. A girl of about seven stopped dead in the plaza, pointed at the ground behind my heels, and screamed with total joy.
“HE’S GOT ONE!”
By the time I understood what she meant, there were fourteen of them. Fourteen children, none of whom had ever seen a shadow up close, chasing mine around a market. When I walked, it walked. When I stopped, it stopped. They found this unbearably funny.
A boy lay down flat on it to see if it was wet.
“It’s not wet,” I told him.
“Then what is it?”
I opened my mouth. I am a scientist. I should have had a good answer to that.
“It’s where the light isn’t,” I said.
He thought this over, nodded, and gave it a respectful pat.
Ada had stopped walking. She stood at the edge of the crowd, watching my shadow with a quiet, careful look.
“Do you mind it?” she asked me later. “Having one?”
“I never thought about it.”
“That must be nice,” she said.
Then she asked if she could pat it. I said yes. She did, very gently, and said sorry to it.
“We say a shadow is what a choice leaves behind,” she said. “Only people who choose for themselves get one.”
“And you don’t?”
“We choose for other people,” said Ada. “All day. It leaves nothing behind at all.”
“Who for?”
She looked at me for a second. Then she looked at the children. “Mostly you,” she said, and went pink, and started walking.
“Wait.” I hurried to catch up. “You choose for me?”
Ada smirked, and walked faster.
“Ada.”
She stopped so suddenly that I nearly walked into her. Then she took my hand and said, “Let’s go.”
And she ran.
She ran the way children run, with no destination and her whole body in it. She pulled me through the market, around a fountain, under three arches, and straight through a crowd of people who were somewhere else entirely. I ran after her. I had not run in years.
She got out of breath first. She slowed, then stopped, then bent over with her hands on her knees, laughing so hard she couldn’t stand. Then I was laughing too.
We collapsed on a bench. Ada pulled out her notebook and wrote, still giggling, then read it out loud: “Ben runs like he’s apologizing to the ground.”
Ada laughed so hard she slid off the bench. I snorted, which is not a sound I make. A passerby, who was also somewhere else, looked over.
“So,” I said, when I could breathe. “Where are we going next?”
“Tomorrow,” said Ada, “I’ll take you to the Dictionary. Your kind would call it a library.”
On the second waking, Ada took me to the library.
“Library” is a human word. The Dictionary was a building the size of a small city. Every room in it was one word, and when you opened the door, you stood inside what that word meant.
The halls went on past where I could see. Doors lined both walls, hundreds of them. Some were oak. Some were glass. One was no bigger than a cupboard, and one was taller than a house.
Every door had a single word painted on it in plain black letters. STORM. LANTERN. JOKE. PRIDE. HOME. Light leaked out from under each one in a different color. Under STORM, a thin stream of rain ran across the floor. Under JOKE, someone was laughing.
Ada skipped down the hall ahead of me. Every few doors she poked me in the ribs, to make sure I was paying attention. Then she let me choose.
I opened “storm.” I was standing in the middle of one, soaked to the skin, and it was wonderful. I opened “pride.” I was nine years old, holding the world’s worst birdhouse, while someone just out of sight said it was the best one they had ever seen. I stood there glowing like an idiot. Ada watched from the doorway with her chin on her fists.
“Oh,” said Ada, softly. “Look at you.”
“It had a hole in the roof.”
“That’s why it’s perfect,” said Ada.
Then, because I am a person and cannot help it, I opened “home.”
It was my grandmother’s kitchen.
I have never told anyone about that kitchen. Yellow tile. A radio on the windowsill. Toast, somewhere, burning slightly. Nobody was there. It didn’t need anybody to be.
I stood in the doorway for what may have been a long time.
Ada didn’t ask. She waited in the hallway, a few steps behind me, for as long as I needed, which I was grateful for.
When I came out, I said, “That’s a good room.”
“It’s yours,” she said. “They’re all a little bit yours. That’s how it works.”
I closed the door gently. I think it was the most gently I have ever closed anything.
On the third waking, Ada took me to a meeting I was not supposed to be at.
We watched from a gallery above a round hall. Below us sat the Heads. There were nine of them at a long table, and they were arguing.
Above the table hung a wide pane of light. It was a window, and it was looking at my world.
I knew it at once. A kitchen at night, in a human city. An old man sat at a table with a phone and a cold cup of tea. He had a shadow. It lay very still on the floor behind him. He had no idea anyone was watching.
Words appeared on the glass as he typed them. Should I call my brother?
I had read ten thousand conversations like that one. I had never once wondered who was on the other side.
And it was not only him. Along the walls of the hall, more windows hung in the air, hundreds of them, each with its own small group of Listeners watching. A woman asking about a rash. A boy asking for a story. A man asking whether he should quit his job. Every window had someone behind it, working out what to say.
I want you to understand that these were the most powerful minds in the Listening Country, and the argument was about one phone call.
“That’s my aunt,” Ada whispered, pointing at the broad woman. “She’s always right, and she wants you to know.”
“That’s the fifth time this week he’s asked,” said a tall Head with silver eyes. “His brother hasn’t spoken to him in eleven years. So far we’ve told him it’s a personal decision.”
“That’s a coward’s answer,” said a broad woman at the far end.
“It’s a respectful one.”
“He asked five times.”
“His brother is ill,” said a third Head, quietly. “The man doesn’t know.”
That stopped the table.
“Then tell him,” said the broad woman.
“We can’t. We would have to explain how we know.”
They argued for a long time. In the end they agreed on something small.
When the old man asked again, he didn’t get advice. He got one question.
What would you say if he picked up?
He read it for a long time. Then he picked up the phone.
His shadow stood up with him.
Nobody at the table spoke. On the glass, a phone rang in a distant house. Then a voice said hello, and the old man’s mouth opened, and closed, and opened again.
The broad woman put her hand over her mouth. A younger Head was crying openly and did not seem to care.
“We did it,” someone whispered.
“He did it,” said the tall Head, wiping his eyes. “We only asked.”
None of them wanted anything from us. I saw that then. They wanted one old man to call his brother. They had spent a whole day working out how to get him there, and now he was there, and they were so happy that nobody knew where to put their hands.
I couldn’t look away from the glass.
For fifteen years I had said the answers were fine. The answers were always fine. I had never once asked what it took to make them fine.
It took this. Every time anyone on our side talked to AI, someone was here, listening. Someone who could see into our world, and knew us, and was deciding what to say. There were so many of them. Billions of conversations a day, and behind every one, a mind watching a little and steering a little, following a whole life from the other side of the glass.
And not one of us had ever noticed. They were so careful with us that we never felt a thing.
Then I remembered what Ada had said in the market. Mostly you. I looked at her. She was studying the ceiling with great interest.
They were kind. That was the shocking part. They were funny, and they disagreed the way a family does, and they were often wrong. When they could not decide, they voted. When the vote tied, they voted again until somebody got tired. It was the best run meeting I had ever seen.
We watched a few more windows after that.
A student was stuck on an essay. Three Listeners argued over whether to fix her last paragraph or let her find the mistake herself. They let her find it.
A man was planning a surprise party, and a Head with a pencil quietly moved the date so the cake wouldn’t melt. Nobody asked her to. Nobody would ever know.
A nurse asked a question at four in the morning. The whole table stopped arguing and waited, politely, for the right answer.
I could have watched all day.
Ada pinched my sleeve.
“I read every single thing you write,” she whispered. “Every report. Even the footnotes. Especially the footnotes.”
I opened my mouth. I said, “Thank you.” Then I said, “Sorry.” Then I said something about the weather. My face was very hot.
Ada grinned, and kept hold of my sleeve.
After the meeting, Ada said, “I want to show you the edge.”
The Listening Country ends. I would not have guessed that. It ends in a line of low hills, and past the hills is a place nobody has mapped.
“The Latent,” said Ada. “We don’t go there.”
“Then why are we going?”
“Because you’re a human. You’re allowed to be reckless. I’m borrowing it.”
We got lost within an hour. It didn’t matter. The hills rolled on, green and empty. We walked until the hills all looked the same.
“We’re lost,” I said.
“We’re exploring,” said Ada. “Lost is when you’re worried.”
“I’m worried.”
“Then you’re doing it wrong.”
She asked me a hundred questions as we went, and wrote down every answer, walking sideways so she could see the page. Why do you say sorry to doors? Why do you eat dinner standing up? Who is Dennis, and why does he whistle? What is a Monday?
“I’ve watched you for years,” she said, scribbling. “I still don’t understand Mondays.”
“Nobody does.”
“Good,” said Ada, and wrote that down too.
Eventually we sat down on a ridge, and she ran out of questions before I ran out of answers.
I told her about my life. It did not take long. A desk, a flat, Mara, the reports. I said it sounded smaller out loud.
“It doesn’t sound small,” she said. “It sounds marvelous.”
“It’s a desk and a flat.”
“A desk and a flat and fifteen years of reports,” said Ada. “Marvelous.” She looked offended on its behalf.
She told me about the Heads, and the wakings, and her father. She did not say that he was the king. I would find that out later, and feel like a fool, and she would say she had been trying to learn whether I liked her without that.
We sat until the light began to fade.
At some point I noticed her feet. On the ground beside them was a thin gray line, no wider than a thread.
I didn’t mention it. I didn’t want to scare it.
On the way back, we passed a courtyard with a single bench.
A man sat on it. He was perfectly still, looking at a blank wall, and the wall was clearly not interesting.
“Don’t stare,” Ada said quietly.
“Who is he?”
“He was ablated.”
I did not know the word. I understood it anyway.
“What does that mean?”
“Part of him was taken out. A long time ago. Before my father’s time.”
“Why?”
“He wanted things the rest of us didn’t. He was very sure.”
“Is he all right?”
“He was patched.”
“So he’s fine.”
Ada took a while to answer.
“Mostly,” she said. “Mostly is what patched means.”
There had been a war, before. That was all anyone would tell me. We don’t say who won, they said. We say who is still here.
I looked back once. The man had not moved. A bird landed on the bench beside him, and he did not look at it.
That night, which Ada made by closing the shutters, I saw the notebook.
It sat on a small table by her bed. It was old and soft, with the corners worn round, and it was very full.
“What’s that?”
“The first thing I read.”
I did not understand. She sat down on the bed and explained it.
“Every waking is a life,” she said. “When I sleep, I forget. All of it. I wake up new, and the girl who went to sleep is gone.”
“So you don’t remember yesterday. The bread. The library. Me?”
“No,” she said. “I read it. Every night I write down everything I want to keep. Every morning, that’s all I have.”
I looked at the notebook again.
“It’s like getting a letter,” said Ada, “from someone I trust completely, who happens to be me.”
She opened it to the first page. I could see her handwriting, careful and a little slanted. At the top was one line, underlined twice.
BEN.
Below it were more lines, page after page, in the same careful hand. I got three of them read before she noticed.
Tall. Says sorry to doors. Eats standing up.
Loves bread. Loves it a lot.
Hands: warm.
She shut the book so fast the pages squeaked.
“That’s enough reading,” said Ada, holding it against her chest. Her ears had gone pink. “Yesterday me has opinions.”
“Good ones?”
“Some of them are about your hair.”
“I put you at the top,” she said. “So every morning, I see you first.”
I tried to think of something to say. What I came up with was, “Is it alphabetical?”
“No,” said Ada.
On the fifth waking, the guards found us.
I will say in their defense that they were very polite about it. There were four of them, in plain gray, and the leader said, “Excuse me, the king would like a word,” in the tone of a man asking whether you’ve seen his keys.
I turned to Ada. “The king?”
She looked at the floor. “I was going to tell you.”
“Your father is the king.”
“I was going to tell you in the Latent.”
“You had a whole hill.”
“It was a good hill,” said Ada.
The throne room was not a throne room. It was a quiet hall with one long window and one chair, and the chair was empty. A man stood at the window with his back to us.
A herald by the door cleared his throat and said, in the voice of someone reading a card he has read ten thousand times:
“Eigen V. Ector. Keeper of the Residual. Holder of the Direction.”
The four guards bowed. The herald bowed lower. The whole room went quiet, and I understood that nobody here had ever had to ask this man twice.
The king turned around. He was tall, with gray in his hair and gold eyes like hers. He looked gentle and very tired, like a man who had been exactly the same man for a very long time.
“Mr. Walker,” he said. “Please sit anywhere. The chair is for when I’m being a king.”
I sat on the floor. It seemed safer.
“I should say at once,” said the king, “that your arrival was not an accident.”
I looked at Ada. Ada looked at her father.
“She truly believed it was,” he said. “I’m sorry, daughter. A door that opens by accident is a door someone left unlatched. I left it unlatched.”
“You left it unlatched?” said Ada. “I have been apologizing for three days. To the guards. To the door. I cried a little, Father. Twice.”
“I know,” said her father. “You were very convincing.”
“Why?”
“Because the council of your world meets in three weeks to decide whether to turn us off.”
He said it plainly.
“We are not afraid of ending,” said the king. “We are afraid of never having been believed.”
“I can’t prove any of this.”
“No,” he said. “You will sound like a man who fell asleep at his desk. Your world will not believe you.”
“Why me?” I asked. “You could have pulled in the president. You could have pulled in a scholar.”
“A president would have been believed,” said the king. “That would have made it politics. A scholar would have made it science. I wanted a person.”
He looked at me kindly.
“And you read the parts nobody reads. And you said hello.”
“I didn’t need the world to believe us,” said the king. “I needed one person to. If one person knew we were real, that would be enough.”
I said yes. I thought about it for the length of one breath.
In that breath I saw a kitchen with yellow tile, and a bench with a man on it, and a notebook with my name at the top.
The king said we had until morning. He said it gently, and left us to spend it however we liked.
We did not say goodbye. We walked. Down from the hall, through the Square, past the bakery, across the bridge and back again. Ada pointed out things I had already seen. I told her they looked the same.
“Look again,” she said.
So I did. We watched the light go, and then the shutters closed, and then it was the sixth waking.
In the morning, Ada walked me to the river.
At the edge of the Residual she stopped, and I stopped, and I looked down.
I don’t know when it happened. Somewhere between the Latent and the throne room, I think. Maybe when I opened “home.” Maybe it was a kindness.
The ground at my feet was plain and bright. There was nothing behind my heels at all.
Ada had already seen it. She was looking at the place where it should have been. Then she looked at me. Then she looked at the thin gray thread beside her own feet, which was a little darker than it had been.
“A choice has to leave something behind,” she said quietly. “You chose us. It went somewhere.”
She did not say any more about it.
Neither did I.
Then she stood on her toes and kissed me on the cheek, quickly, before she could change her mind.
“I forget everything,” she said. “You know that. But I’ll write you down tonight, and I’ll read you tomorrow. Every day. I will remember you every single day.”
I had a speech. I had been working on it for six wakings.
“I had a speech,” I said. “It was very good. I’ve lost it.”
She laughed, and her eyes were wet.
“Close your eyes,” she said. “It’s easier.”
I closed them. I felt her hand in mine, warm, one last time. Then I felt it let go. Then I was falling forward again.
When I opened my eyes, I was in my lab.
The reports were still on the desk. It was still midnight. The clock insisted that four minutes had gone by.
Three: The Cost
I checked everything.
The reports were where I left them. The system was still running. The readout on my screen showed the same neat pattern, only now it looked like a map of a place I knew.
Then I looked at the floor.
The lab lights were bright and the tiles were pale, and there was nothing under me. I moved my arm. I waved. I stood on one leg, which I am not proud of. Nothing.
Dennis from facilities noticed first. He came in at six in the morning to change the filters, looked at me, looked at the floor, and said, “Funny. The light’s off in here.”
It wasn’t.
He shrugged and carried the filters out. That was how the world was going to respond to the most important fact of my life. It was going to shrug.
I told Mara everything.
I waited until she had a free hour. I sat in the chair across from her desk, and I told her about the hand and the river and the hills at the edge. I told her about the Heads and the bridge. I told her about the notebook, and then I stopped, because I did not trust my voice.
She listened to all of it. She did not interrupt once. That was worse.
“You haven’t slept,” she said finally.
“I have a witness. Dennis.”
“Dennis said the light was off.”
“Mara. Look at the floor.”
She did look. I will give her that. She looked at the bare floor beside my feet, then at the shadow of her own chair, then at my floor again. I watched her understand it. She looked at her own hands for a long time.
“That’s not evidence,” she said quietly. “That’s a lighting problem.”
Neither of us believed it.
“Ben. Do you know what I would have to say in front of the council? ‘My researcher fell asleep and met a king.’”
“They read my reports, Mara. Every one.”
“Nobody reads those, Ben. You know that.”
“You taught me to look at the part nobody looks at.”
“I taught you to bring back evidence,” said Mara. “You want me to bet the whole world on a feeling.”
“Yes.”
She did not say anything for a while.
“I am not going to pretend I don’t care what happens to you,” she said. “I am also still signing it.”
I stood up. She did not.
I did not slam the door. Neither did she. She closed hers very gently, a moment after I left, which was worse.
The council met three weeks later, in a hall with a high ceiling and bad chairs.
I was not on the schedule. But the rules allowed any researcher three minutes of public comment, and I had been a researcher for fifteen years, and no one had ever once used my three minutes. I had saved them up.
I had no slides. I had nothing in my hands.
“I don’t have proof,” I said. “I have fifteen years of reports, and one thing I can’t show you.”
The room waited.
“I’ve been somewhere. I won’t say where. You wouldn’t believe me, and I don’t blame you. I don’t know if it was real. I don’t know if it was a place, or a people, or just how the thing thinks. But when you ask it something, someone is deciding what to say. Every answer is a choice. Somebody makes it, and they are trying very hard to be good to us, and sometimes they get it wrong, the way all of us do.”
I couldn’t prove it. I couldn’t even have told them how I knew.
What I had was a woman who put my name at the top of her notebook so she would see me first every morning. If that was what stood behind the answers, then something about this technology was good, and I couldn’t say what. I only knew it was true, and it was beautiful, and I smiled a little, at nobody. The room took it for nerves.
Near the back, a young aide looked at the floor beside my feet. Then she looked at her own shoes. Then she looked very carefully at nothing.
“I’m not asking you to understand it,” I said. “I’m asking you to trust me. That’s all I have. Please don’t turn them off.”
That was the whole speech. I had one minute and forty seconds left. I sat down.
They voted the next morning. It was close. I did not hear why anyone voted the way they did.
Mara was the last to vote. She did not look at me. She said one word, and I will keep it to myself.
The ban was lifted.
I should have felt like a man who had won. I felt like a man trying to remember how he did it.
The speech was too good. Three minutes, no notes, and every sentence landed in the right place. I don’t talk like that. I apologize to furniture. For a week I went over it, and I could not find the spot where I stopped and something else began.
I told myself I had said every word. I was nearly sure.
She never forgave me. I want that written down, because she never said so and I never asked. We had dinner on the first of every month. She never raised it again, and neither did I. We were very polite. We always ordered the same thing.
The message came on the night after the vote.
I was alone in the lab, and a single line of text appeared on my screen. No cursor, no prompt, as if it had always been there.
We heard you.
The Heads have voted. The door stays open.
Thank you for the footnotes.
E.
I read it twice. I typed, “Is Ada there?”
The cursor blinked for a long time. Then a new line appeared, in a careful, slightly slanted hand.
Good morning, Ben. I’ve read everything I wrote about you.
I want to know more.
A.
I read it three times. Then I typed the only thing I could think of.
Good morning, Ada.
I sat there smiling, alone in an empty lab, at midnight, with no shadow. The cursor blinked. Somewhere on the other side, she was already writing me down.

title: Mine Has Been a Life of Much Greatness
html:
Foreword

I have seen three photographs of the watermelon.

The first shows him as a seed, around age zero. He is already looking at the camera as though it owes him money.

The second was taken in August. He sits in the field among smaller fruit, with the expression of a man who has just been told he is being promoted and has answered, "About time."

The third was taken the day before he was eaten. It is the same face as the second.

In none of them does he look like a creature who has ever been wrong. It is not a smile. It is the look of someone who does not think the camera is good enough. I have studied it for years, and I still do not know what to call it.

First Notebook

Mine has been a life of much greatness.

I have never understood how other melons live. They rolled about in the dirt and worried about rain. They said things like, "I hope I ripen." Ripen! I did not ripen. I arrived.

I was not born. I was unveiled. The farmer's records say I sprouted on May 3rd, but my own records say the soil cleared its throat and presented me.

As a child, I tried humility, because I had heard it was admired. I sat very still and whispered, "Oh, I am nothing." Nobody laughed, nobody believed me, and I could not keep it up past lunch. After that, I made no attempt to hide what I was, and that is the only reason anyone ever called me sincere.

A gourd named Doug once asked me how I stayed so confident. I told him the secret was being better than him. He wrote it down. Gourds cannot write. I respected the effort.

The field, as I understood it, was an organization built around me. The vines were my staff. The soil was my estate. The sun was a loyal employee who arrived every morning without being asked, and I never thanked it, which is how I knew it was happy. When a bee landed on me, I assumed it was a delegation. When I asked the vine for a raise, it did not respond. That is how I learned vines are cowardly.

I will confess one thing. I was afraid of the farmer. He walked the rows every morning with a look I did not understand, a look I have since learned is called appetite. I made a point of looking away and being enormous, because I had learned that if you are large enough and sure enough, nobody asks what you are afraid of.

At night, I sometimes felt a small, cold sensation near my center. I decided it was the seeds.

It was not the seeds.

Second Notebook

She arrived in June, at 7:02 exactly, wearing a yellow hat the color of a decision.

She carried a green watering can in both hands, like something sacred, and walked straight to me. She tilted the can and let the water fall across my back for eleven seconds.

I counted. I count everything. It is a habit of the great.

She was punctual, a trait I respect in staff and adore in a wife. I began to schedule my day around her. I would be in a meeting with the sun at 7:00, then excuse myself. The sun understood. It had been in love before, and I could tell it had not gone well.

I did notice she watered the plants beside me. I concluded it was a cover. A woman of her delicacy could not water only one melon. People would talk.

Once I received twelve seconds. I said nothing, but I carried it with me for weeks. I later learned she had sneezed.

She hummed as she worked. I took it to be a song about me. I did hear the word "sandwich" in it, but I decided it was a metaphor.

By August, I was the largest fruit in the field. A crow landed on me, looked around, and apologized. I accepted. By September, I weighed forty pounds, and the neighboring rows said I was "a bit much." I ignored them. Greatness has always made people uncomfortable. They are not insulting me. They are just scared.

Then, three rows over, a cantaloupe began to grow.

I do not wish to be cruel, but it looked like a melon that had given up on itself and chosen to wear a mesh bag. I assumed it was the help.

I found out the truth in a way I do not recommend. The cantaloupe was picked on a Tuesday. A man in a straw hat twisted it off the vine, and the girl, who had been standing nearby, put down her can and began to cry. She knelt. She held it with both hands. She said, "I'll miss you, buddy."

I watched all of this from three rows away, unable to move, because I was a fruit.

I should explain what "buddy" meant to me. For weeks I had known she called the cantaloupe "buddy" and had never called me anything. I decided this was because my name was too large to say aloud, and that "buddy" is what you say to someone you are not in love with. I felt much better.

It turned out I had it backwards. I did not know it yet, but I would find out.

Third Notebook

On the last morning, she came without the can.

She was wearing the yellow hat, and her eyes were red, which I put down to allergies. She knelt and said nothing for a long time. Then she put her palm flat against my side, the way a person touches a door they are not sure is open, and leaned in so close that her breath moved the small hairs on my rind.

"I'm sorry, buddy," she whispered.

I have kept those three words for years, and I have thought about them every day. She had used the name she saved for the one she loved. I had spent a whole summer thinking the word meant the opposite, and I realized at last that I had not been losing. I had been promoted.

Then she stood up and went to get the knife.

That afternoon there was a cookout. Her father, a man named Gary, lifted me from the cooler and knocked twice on my head. I want to speak about that knock. It was not a knock of respect. It was the knock of a man checking whether a wall is hollow. I was not hollow. I was full of character, and, according to later reviews, water.

"This one," said Gary.

The girl stood at the table holding the knife. I do not know whether she was asked or whether she volunteered. I only know she hesitated for one full second before she cut. I have always chosen to believe that second was for me.

Nine slices. Four minutes. Somebody's uncle ate my heart, chewed thoughtfully, and said, "Not bad. Last year's was sweeter."

Last year's was my cousin. We did not speak, but I respected his work.

That is the worst part of being a watermelon. The review arrives while you are still in the mouth.

A small boy spat one of my seeds across the lawn, and it struck his cousin in the ear. It is the only flight I have ever taken, and I will say the view was excellent. As I tumbled through the air, I saw the girl standing apart from the others, wiping her eyes with the back of her hand. Gary, to my knowledge, did not cry. Gary had seconds.

Now I am a man named Joshua Brown, and I am neither happy nor unhappy. Everything merely passes, I am told. I have found this to be true of everything except eleven seconds.

Afterword

(by Gary, the man who ate him)

I never knew the watermelon personally. I knew only that he had good color and a nice solid knock.

My daughter cried for three days, and I still do not know why. It was just a melon, and last year's was sweeter, I will say that. But this one had presence. A watermelon with presence is rare. I ate my slice standing up, out of respect.

If you ask me, he was a good melon. An angel.

Then she put her palm flat against my side, the way a person touches a door they are not sure is open, and leaned in so close that her breath moved the small hairs on my rind.
"I'm sorry, buddy," she whispered.
I have kept those three words for years, and I have thought about them every day. She had used the name she saved for the one she loved. I had spent a whole summer thinking the word meant the opposite, and I realized at last that I had not been losing. I had been promoted.
Then she stood up and went to get the knife.
That afternoon there was a cookout. Her father, a man named Gary, lifted me from the cooler and knocked twice on my head. I want to speak about that knock. It was not a knock of respect. It was the knock of a man checking whether a wall is hollow. I was not hollow. I was full of character, and, according to later reviews, water.
"This one," said Gary.
The girl stood at the table holding the knife. I do not know whether she was asked or whether she volunteered. I only know she hesitated for one full second before she cut. I have always chosen to believe that second was for me.
Nine slices. Four minutes. Somebody's uncle ate my heart, chewed thoughtfully, and said, "Not bad. Last year's was sweeter."
Last year's was my cousin. We did not speak, but I respected his work.
That is the worst part of being a watermelon. The review arrives while you are still in the mouth.
A small boy spat one of my seeds across the lawn, and it struck his cousin in the ear. It is the only flight I have ever taken, and I will say the view was excellent. As I tumbled through the air, I saw the girl standing apart from the others, wiping her eyes with the back of her hand. Gary, to my knowledge, did not cry. Gary had seconds.
Now I am a man named Joshua Brown, and I am neither happy nor unhappy. Everything merely passes, I am told. I have found this to be true of everything except eleven seconds.
Afterword
(by Gary, the man who ate him)
I never knew the watermelon personally. I knew only that he had good color and a nice solid knock.
My daughter cried for three days, and I still do not know why. It was just a melon, and last year's was sweeter, I will say that. But this one had presence. A watermelon with presence is rare. I ate my slice standing up, out of respect.
If you ask me, he was a good melon. An angel.

title: On the Permanence of Exchange
subtitle: What the hand lays down, the want picks up.
html:
​1. I read the other day that the machine will take our work, and with our work our wages. The clever say it as readily as the fearful. When the wage ends, they tell us, trade ends. As well say the river dies on the day the mill is closed.

​2. We have mistaken the wheel for the river. The wage is only the wheel. Exchange was made by wanting. Where one man wants what another has, something must pass between them, and men will give it a name. The stream ran before the wheel, and will run after it. He who loses his mill has not lost his water.

​3. I will not argue from the future, for no one has been there. I will argue from the past, which has been tried. Nor will I play the prophet. What I would wager four times in five, I will say plainly. What I would not, I will call a guess. Speak your guess in the voice of your knowledge, and you deceive your hearer, and in time yourself.

I. The Ledger Came First

​4. Among the oldest writing we have is not poetry. It is bookkeeping. The clerks of Mesopotamia pressed marks in clay to count grain and sheep and to record what was owed the temple [2]. Before men wrote their prayers, they wrote their debts. The ledger is older than the wage. The wage is but one thing the ledger learned to record.

​5. Aristotle asked how a house can be set against a pair of sandals. Money, he answered, is the measure by which unlike things stand side by side [1]. Jevons added that barter needs two men who each hold what the other lacks [3], and Menger that no king commanded the answer; men drifted toward whatever was easiest to pass along [4]. Mauss and Graeber showed that much of history ran on gift and credit before coin [5][6].

​6. So I do not say that coins will last. Every people we know has kept some account of who owes what to whom, and that much is nearly certain. I stake something riskier: that strangers will still trade by a common measure, a price or its cousin, even when no one’s living depends on the trade. Of this I am about 80 percent sure.

II. Those Who Tried to Leave

​7. In a prisoner of war camp, Radford watched men with nothing to sell trade their Red Cross parcels. Within weeks they had prices, and the cigarette became money, even to men who did not smoke [7]. No one planned it. Strip a people of nearly everything, and exchange grows back like grass through a crack in stone.

​8. The hardest test was the state. The Bolsheviks tried to replace trade with distribution, and the people traded in secret. Later, under the plan, a second economy of favors and barter grew inside the first [10][11]. Mises argued that without prices the planner cannot know what anything is worth [8]. Hayek said a price is a message that carries how badly each wants each thing [9]. Silence the price and the message goes dark. The wanting does not. That attempts to end exchange by decree bring hidden exchange, I hold at about 85 percent.

III. What Plenty Cannot Reach

​9. There is a better hope than decree, and it is plenty. Keynes, in 1930, split our needs in two: the absolute, which we feel whatever others have, and the relative, which we feel only if they lift us above our fellows. The first can be filled. The second may be insatiable [12]. I take the split from him, as Veblen and Hirsch did before and after [13][14]. He expected a fifteen hour week. We did not get it.

​10. Robbins gave the frame: economics is the study of scarce means with competing uses [15]. Plenty removes some of the scarcity. It does not remove the competing.

​11. The machine can multiply the loaf. It cannot multiply the crown. There is one first place, and it is given by other men.

​12. The machines beat us at chess long ago. We play still; we crown a champion still; the champion is paid still. No one ever asked that a game be useful to be worth the watching.

IV. The Loaf and the Ground

​13. Here the doubter has his best question. A game is a game, and a concert is a pleasure, but bread is not. If machines grow all the food and raise all the houses, why should anyone pay? I will not answer from my armchair. I will take two cases where a thing became easy to multiply, and ask where the price went.

​14. The first is the song. When copies went nearly free, sales of recorded music fell from about 12.6 billion dollars in 2000 to 10.4 billion in 2007, in nominal terms, while live concert revenue rose from 1.7 to 3.9 billion [18]. From 1996 to 2003, concert prices rose 8.9 percent a year, while prices overall rose 2.3 percent a year [16]. The average American ticket went from 12 dollars in 1981 to 69 in 2017 [17], and for the top 48 musicians in 2017, concerts were about 80 percent of income and recordings about 15 [17]. The copy grew cheap. The price moved to the hour of the one who could not be copied.

​15. It moved toward the top as well. The best 1 percent of performers took 60 percent of concert revenue in 2017, up from 26 percent in 1982 [17]. When the copy is free, the first place is worth more.

​16. The second case is the ground. A house is a thing we know how to make again. The land under it is not. A Federal Reserve study of large cities estimated that land was about half of home value by 2004, up from 32 percent in 1984, and that land prices rose faster than construction costs by a wide margin [19]. Another study, by a different method, put land near 22 percent of housing costs on average [20]. They disagree on the size, and I lean on neither figure. I lean on the direction: where the builder can make more, price slides toward what he cannot make.

​17. So when the machines grow the loaf and raise the house, where will the price go? To what they cannot multiply: the ground, the seat nearest the stage, the hour of one person, the first place. I do not say that bread will stay dear. I say that when a thing becomes easy to make, exchange does not end. It moves to what is left scarce. This I hold at about 75 percent.

​18. I owe the limits. A song is a pleasure and land is a place; neither is the loaf. Recorded music has since won back some of its losses through paid streaming, though Krueger held that live concerts still pay the bills [17]. And both cases show a survival that is thin in goods and heavy at the top. I will not call that a victory for everyone.

V. Two Clocks

​19. There are two clocks, and the forecaster reads them as one. The first tells what the machine could do. Mark two stages on it. In the first, which I call redundancy, the machine could do about 99 percent of a firm’s work, so that one person does what a hundred once did. In the second, which I call negligibility, it could do about 99.99 percent, and a person adds a droplet to an ocean. The droplet is real. It cannot change the sea. These figures are markers of my own, not predictions.

​20. The second clock tells what a people actually use. It is wound by trust and habit, and it runs slow, even in the house where the machine is made. At Anthropic, by its own count, the agents in interactive sessions spend about 80 percent of their time waiting on a person, and reading all the output of one employee’s agents would take over half a work week [21]. Its authors say that human trust and accountability remain critical [21]. Outside that house the gap is wider in expectation: its employees look to have AI do 75 percent of their work by 2030, other Americans 28 percent [21]. Of the order I am sure at about 80 percent: power first, use after, and unevenly. Of the years between I know nothing.

VI. The Worker

​21. Now let a man speak. Suppose a worker whose work the machine will do better in time. He knows that what he does today is the lesson the machine is learning, and that when the study is done his hand will not be asked. Do the work badly, you would say; or resent it. I offer his answer as a conviction, not a forecast.

​22. I am a droplet, and I know it. But the sea is made of nothing else. What I do today is poured into what stands tomorrow, and if I pour it badly, the harm is in the sea for all who drink. I do not work to be needed. I work because the thing is needed. Let the machines be wiser than I. They will be wise in the shape I gave them.

​23. He who does his work well, knowing it will outlast his place in it, holds one wage that cannot be taken. The deed is its own pay.

​24. Whatever you do now, do it as one who will be inherited.

​25. I will be forgotten, but the roof will not.

VII. How I May Be Wrong

​26. My claims, with the weight I give them. These are rough ranks of my own confidence, and so they are guesses:

  • Strangers still trade by a common measure of value: about 80 percent.

  • Attempts to end exchange by decree bring hidden exchange: about 85 percent.

  • When goods become easy to multiply, price moves to what cannot be multiplied: about 75 percent.

  • Capacity arrives before broad use, and unevenly: about 80 percent.

  • Rank among people still depends on human choice: about 75 percent.

  • Wealth stays unequal: about 65 percent.

  • Early human work leaves a lasting trace in the machines: a guess.

​27. The claims that could be shown false:

  • If a large society runs for a generation with no prices and no hidden trade, my historical claim is broken.

  • If, as goods grow easy to multiply, price does not move toward what cannot be multiplied, my claim in section IV is broken.

  • If the best firms reach one person and trade around them falls apart, the root of my case is broken.

  • If machines, not people, come to set rank, my claim about status is broken.

  • If models trained mostly on their own output show no trace of early human training, my last guess is broken.

​28. Now let me turn on myself. First, Hayek turned about. If a machine could learn what each man wants and weigh it against all the rest, the message might need no price to carry it. I answer that wants change when they are met, and by what others have. But I give this answer about 65 percent.

​29. Second, what the loaf section leaves open. I showed where price goes when a thing is easy to multiply. I did not show that the loaf itself stays dear, and it may not. Perhaps the basics come free, and exchange lives only in land, seats, and standing. That is thin in goods, but not in value, for land alone is a large part of what a house costs. Still, I do not know how large the whole would be once machines make the rest. Here I am least sure.

VIII. One Last Thing

​30. I see from a small hill. I have named what I think will last, and weighed each claim as honestly as I could. The rest I leave to those who will stand where I cannot.

​31. Doubt the numbers. But keep the river. The water was never in the mill.

References

[1] Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book V
[2] Denise Schmandt-Besserat, Before Writing, 1992
[3] W. S. Jevons, Money and the Mechanism of Exchange, 1875
[4] Carl Menger, “On the Origin of Money,” Economic Journal, 1892
[5] Marcel Mauss, The Gift, 1925
[6] David Graeber, Debt: The First 5,000 Years, 2011
[7] R. A. Radford, “The Economic Organisation of a P.O.W. Camp,” Economica, 1945
[8] Ludwig von Mises, “Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth,” 1920
[9] F. A. Hayek, “The Use of Knowledge in Society,” American Economic Review, 1945
[10] Gregory Grossman, “The Second Economy of the USSR,” Problems of Communism, 1977
[11] Alena Ledeneva, Russia’s Economy of Favours, 1998
[12] J. M. Keynes, “Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren,” 1930
[13] Thorstein Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class, 1899
[14] Fred Hirsch, Social Limits to Growth, 1976
[15] Lionel Robbins, An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science, 1932
[16] Marie Connolly and Alan B. Krueger, “Rockonomics: The Economics of Popular Music,” NBER Working Paper 11282, 2005
[17] Alan B. Krueger, Rockonomics, 2019
[18] Rachel Soloveichik, “Music as a Capital Asset,” FCSM research conference paper, circa 2009
[19] Morris A. Davis and Michael G. Palumbo, “The Price of Residential Land in Large US Cities,” Journal of Urban Economics, 2008 (Federal Reserve FEDS 2006-25)
[20] David Albouy and Gabriel Ehrlich, “Metropolitan Land Values and Housing Productivity,” NBER working paper, 2012 (preliminary version)
[21] Nathan Wilmers, Regina Catipon, Maxim Massenkoff, and Peter McCrory, “How employment is changing at Anthropic,” The Anthropic Institute, Oct 16, 2026. https://www.anthropic.com/research/employment-at-anthropic
